SOAPSTone & the Rhetorical Situation

Speaker
Who is writing/speaking, and what do we know about them?
Occasion
What event or context prompted this text?
Audience
Who is the writer specifically trying to reach?
Purpose
Always phrased as 'to ___' — the intended effect
Subject
What the text is specifically about
Tone
The writer's attitude toward the subject
Exigence
The urgent problem making the writing necessary now

The Three Appeals

AppealTargetsBuilt through
EthosCredibilityCredentials, fairness, careful language
PathosEmotionVivid imagery, anecdotes, charged language
LogosLogicStatistics, data, clear reasoning

Common Rhetorical Devices

Anaphora
Repetition at the START of successive clauses
Epistrophe
Repetition at the END of successive clauses
Antithesis
Contrasting ideas in parallel structure
Chiasmus
Reversed grammatical structure across clauses
Juxtaposition
Placing two things side by side to highlight contrast
Metaphor
Direct comparison, no 'like/as'
Simile
Comparison using 'like' or 'as'
Hyperbole
Deliberate exaggeration for effect
Understatement
Deliberately downplaying for effect
Anadiplosis
Repeating a clause's last word to start the next

Common Logical Fallacies

FallacyWhat it does
Ad hominemAttacks the person, not the argument
Straw manMisrepresents an argument as weaker to attack it
False dilemmaPresents only two options when more exist
Slippery slopeClaims one step inevitably leads to an extreme end
Hasty generalizationDraws a broad conclusion from too small a sample

The Three Essay Types

EssayCore task
SynthesisYour argument, using ≥3 provided sources as support
Rhetorical AnalysisHOW a writer builds their argument, not whether you agree
ArgumentYour position, defended with your own evidence — no provided sources

Fast Facts

  • Always follow "device identified" with "here's its effect" — labeling alone earns little credit.
  • Subject is what a text is about; purpose is what it wants to accomplish — never confuse the two.
  • Commentary explains WHY evidence matters; summary just restates WHAT it says.
  • A comma splice needs a period, semicolon, or conjunction — not just a deleted comma.
  • Parallel structure means every item in a list shares the same grammatical form.
  • On MC questions, always verify your answer against the actual passage text.
memoryHtml:
Quick ways to lock in the facts you keep forgetting. Read the big trick, then the small note tells you what it unlocks. Say them out loud — silly is memorable.

Rhetorical Situation

Purpose is a verb, not a noun
Never write "the purpose is technology" — write "to warn readers about..." If it's not phrased as "to ___," it isn't purpose yet.
Subject ≠ Purpose
Subject is WHAT it's about. Purpose is what the writer wants to happen because of it. Two totally different questions, always answer both.

Appeals & Fallacies

E-P-L: Ethics, Passion, Logic
Ethos=credibility (think "ethics"). Pathos=emotion (think "passion" or "sympathy"). Logos=logic (think "logical").
Name it, then explain it
"This is pathos" earns nothing alone. Always finish the sentence: "...which makes the audience feel ___, moving them to ___."
Attack the argument, not the arguer
If the criticism is about the PERSON instead of their actual claim, it's probably ad hominem, not real logos.

Devices

Anaphora starts, epistrophe ends
Anaphora repeats at the BEGINNING of clauses. Epistrophe repeats at the END. Both start with vowels near the front of the alphabet — 'a' comes before 'e,' just like 'anaphora' comes at the start.
Simile has the 'like/as' sibling
'Simile' sounds like 'similar' — it's a comparison, and it always keeps the word 'like' or 'as' as a visible sibling.

Style

Short = sharp, long = layered
Short sentences hit hard and fast. Long sentences build, accumulate, and layer ideas on top of each other.
Ban vague tone words
If your tone word could describe a hundred different passages ('good,' 'bad,' 'interesting'), it's too vague — get specific.

Argument Building

"So what?" after every quote
Every time you cite evidence, silently ask yourself "so what?" — the answer to that question IS your commentary.
Concede, then pivot
"Sure, X has a point, BUT..." is the whole shape of a concession-rebuttal — acknowledge fairly, then turn back to your claim.

The Three Essays

Synthesis = your argument + their sources
Never summarize sources in order. Build YOUR claims first, then drop sources in as support — like citations in a research paper, not a book report.
Rhetorical analysis = HOW, not IF
You are never arguing whether the writer is right. You are only explaining how they built their case and why it works.
Argument = your evidence, no packet
No sources are given — dig into history, current events, or your own experience for real, specific proof.

Grammar

A comma alone can't join two sentences
Two complete sentences need a period, a semicolon, or a comma PLUS a conjunction (and/but/so) — a lone comma creates a splice.
Match the list's grammar
If one item in a series ends in '-ing,' they all should. Mismatched forms in a list is a parallel structure error.

units.name: The Rhetorical Situation

concepts.intro: Every piece of writing happens inside a specific situation — SOAPSTone is a checklist for reading that situation before you analyze anything else.
b: Speaker: who is writing or speaking, and what do we know about their background, authority, or perspective?
Occasion: what event, moment, or context prompted this piece of writing?
Audience: who is the writer specifically trying to reach or persuade?
Purpose: what does the writer want the audience to think, feel, or do as a result?
Subject: what is the piece actually about, stated as specifically as possible?
Tone: the writer's attitude toward the subject, revealed through word choice and style.

concepts.intro: Exigence is the specific problem, need, or urgency that makes a piece of writing necessary right now.
b: Every argument responds to something — a controversy, an event, a gap in public understanding.
Identifying the exigence helps explain WHY the writer chose this moment and this approach.
Exigence is different from subject: the subject is what the text is about; the exigence is why it needed to be written.

concepts.intro: Writers don't create in a vacuum — the situation itself shapes what choices are even available to them.
b: Context includes the historical moment, medium (speech, essay, ad), and cultural setting a text is produced in.
Constraints are limits on the writer: word count, audience expectations, what is considered appropriate for the occasion.
A skilled writer works within constraints rather than ignoring them — this is part of what you analyze.

concepts.intro: Confusing what a text is ABOUT with what it is trying to DO is one of the most common early mistakes in rhetorical reading.
b: Subject answers 'what is this about?' Purpose answers 'what does the writer want to happen because of this?'
Two texts can share a subject (e.g., climate change) but have completely different purposes (to alarm, to reassure, to mobilize, to inform).
Always state purpose as an infinitive verb phrase: 'to persuade,' 'to criticize,' 'to celebrate' — not as a noun.

concepts.intro: Every text is shaped by the relationship among the writer, the audience, and the subject, at a particular moment.
b: The rhetorical triangle links speaker (ethos), audience (pathos), and message/subject (logos).
Kairos is the opportune moment: the right argument delivered at the right time to the right people.
A response ignores kairos when it is technically sound but poorly timed or aimed.
Exigence supplies the 'why now'; kairos supplies the 'why this approach, at this moment'.
On the exam, name the rhetorical situation precisely before analyzing choices.

concepts.intro: Effective writers shape appeals around what a specific audience knows, values, and needs.
b: Identify the audience's likely assumptions, values, and level of prior knowledge.
A hostile audience calls for concession and shared premises before disagreement.
A sympathetic audience can be moved to action rather than merely persuaded of a position.
Diction, examples, and tone should all be calibrated to that audience.
Ask: what does this audience need to believe or feel to accept the claim?

traps: Confusing the SUBJECT of a text (what it's about) with its PURPOSE (what it wants to accomplish) — these are always separate questions.
Assuming the audience is 'everyone' — strong rhetorical analysis identifies a SPECIFIC intended audience, even if the text is public.
Describing tone with a vague word like 'negative' instead of a precise one like 'scornful,' 'wistful,' or 'indignant.'
Treating 'audience' as 'anyone who reads it' — analysis must name the specific intended audience.
fms: SOAPSTone: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone
Exigence = the urgent problem that makes the writing necessary now
Purpose is always a verb phrase: 'to ___'
Rhetorical triangle: speaker-audience-subject; kairos = the right message at the right moment.

units.name: Rhetorical Appeals & Logical Fallacies

concepts.intro: Aristotle's three appeals are the foundation of persuasion — almost every argument leans on some combination of the three.
b: Ethos appeals to credibility and character — why should we trust this speaker? Built through expertise, fairness, or shared values.
Pathos appeals to emotion — the writer wants the audience to FEEL something (fear, hope, anger, sympathy) that moves them toward the writer's position.
Logos appeals to logic and reason — facts, statistics, examples, and clear chains of reasoning.

concepts.intro: Ethos isn't just 'the writer is famous' — it's actively constructed within the text itself.
b: Citing credentials or firsthand experience builds ethos by establishing authority.
Acknowledging the opposing side fairly builds ethos by showing the writer is reasonable, not one-sided.
Using precise, careful language (rather than sloppy or inflammatory language) builds ethos through demonstrated competence.

concepts.intro: A fallacy is a flaw in reasoning that makes an argument persuasive-SOUNDING without actually being logically sound.
b: Ad hominem: attacking the person making an argument instead of the argument itself.
Straw man: misrepresenting an opponent's argument as weaker than it really is, then attacking that weak version.
False dilemma (either/or): presenting only two options when more actually exist.
Slippery slope: claiming one small step will inevitably lead to an extreme, unlikely outcome without justifying the chain.
Hasty generalization: drawing a broad conclusion from too small or unrepresentative a sample.

concepts.intro: On the exam, you must be able to point to a SPECIFIC line and name which appeal it uses and why it works.
b: Look for statistics, expert citations, and cause-effect reasoning as signals of logos.
Look for vivid imagery, personal anecdotes, and charged language as signals of pathos.
Look for the writer establishing shared values or referencing their own credibility as signals of ethos.
A single passage often blends more than one appeal — strong analysis explains HOW they work together, not just which is present.

concepts.l: Logos: evidence and forms of reasoning
concepts.intro: Logical appeal rests on the type and arrangement of evidence and inference.
b: Deductive reasoning moves from a general principle to a specific conclusion.
Inductive reasoning builds from specific cases to a general claim (always somewhat provisional).
Evidence types: facts and statistics, expert testimony, anecdotes, analogies, hypothetical examples.
Analogical reasoning is only as strong as the similarity between the two things compared.
Weak logos often shows up as hasty generalization or a false cause (post hoc).

concepts.intro: Ethos includes the character a writer constructs on the page, not just real-world credentials.
b: Persona is the version of the writer the text projects (reasonable, outraged, humble, authoritative).
Word choice, sentence rhythm, and level of formality all build persona.
A shift in persona mid-text is a deliberate rhetorical move worth analyzing.
Self-deprecation or admitting limits can strengthen ethos by signaling honesty.
Analyze persona by asking how the writer wants to be seen and how the language creates that impression.

traps: Simply LABELING an appeal ('this is pathos') without explaining HOW it functions and WHY it's effective earns little credit — always connect device to effect.
Mistaking emotional language for a fallacy — using pathos is not automatically a logical flaw, it's a legitimate rhetorical strategy.
Confusing ad hominem (attacking the person) with a legitimate ethos critique (questioning a source's actual expertise on THIS topic).
Labeling an appeal (pathos!) without explaining the specific words that create it and the effect on the audience.
fms: Ethos = credibility · Pathos = emotion · Logos = logic
Fallacy = a flaw in reasoning that sounds convincing but isn't valid
Always explain HOW a device works, not just that it's present
Deductive = general to specific; inductive = specific to general; persona = the self the text projects.

units.name: Rhetorical Devices & Figurative Language

concepts.intro: Repeating words or structures is one of the most common ways writers create emphasis and rhythm.
b: Anaphora: repetition of a word or phrase at the BEGINNING of successive clauses or sentences ('I have a dream that...').
Epistrophe: repetition at the END of successive clauses ('of the people, by the people, for the people').
Parallelism: repeating a grammatical structure (e.g., a series of matching phrases) to create balance and rhythm.
Anadiplosis: repeating the last word of one clause at the start of the next, linking ideas together.

concepts.intro: Placing ideas in tension with each other is a powerful way to make a point memorable.
b: Antithesis: placing two contrasting ideas in a parallel grammatical structure ('Ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country').
Juxtaposition: placing two things side by side to highlight their differences.
Chiasmus: a reversal of grammatical structure in successive phrases ('ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country' is also chiastic in structure).

concepts.intro: Figurative language asks the reader to understand one thing in terms of another, creating a vivid or persuasive image.
b: Metaphor: a direct comparison without 'like' or 'as' (e.g., 'the classroom was a zoo').
Simile: a comparison using 'like' or 'as.'
Personification: giving human qualities to something nonhuman.
Hyperbole: deliberate exaggeration for effect, not meant to be taken literally.
Understatement: deliberately downplaying something for ironic or persuasive effect.

concepts.intro: Some devices work by NOT stating things directly, forcing the reader to fill in the meaning themselves.
b: A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not to get a literal answer — it leads the reader to a conclusion the writer wants them to reach.
Verbal irony says one thing but means another, often to criticize or add wit.
Sarcasm is a sharp, often mocking form of verbal irony.
Understanding irony requires paying attention to CONTEXT — the same sentence can be sincere or ironic depending on the situation.

concepts.intro: How language sounds and moves shapes emphasis and emotion.
b: Alliteration and assonance bind phrases and make lines memorable.
Asyndeton (omitting conjunctions) speeds a list and can feel urgent or overwhelming.
Polysyndeton (repeating conjunctions) slows a list and can feel weighty or exhausting.
Cadence and sentence length create a rhythm that reinforces tone.
Analyze the effect of the sound, not just its name.

concepts.intro: Comparisons and references import meaning and feeling from elsewhere.
b: Allusion is a brief reference to a shared text, event, or figure, relying on the audience to recognize it.
An effective allusion transfers the authority or emotion of its source to the present argument.
An extended metaphor develops a single comparison across a passage, structuring the reader's understanding.
Analogy argues that because two situations are alike in some ways, they are alike in another.
Always connect the comparison to the writer's purpose.

traps: Naming a device correctly but never explaining its EFFECT on the reader or argument — the AP exam always wants function, not just identification.
Confusing a simile (uses 'like'/'as') with a metaphor (no comparison word) — a small distinction graders check for.
Missing irony because a statement is being read only at face value — always check whether the surrounding context contradicts the literal words.
Identifying a device (anaphora, antithesis) and stopping there, without analyzing what it accomplishes.
fms: Anaphora = repetition at the START of clauses · Epistrophe = repetition at the END
Antithesis = contrasting ideas in parallel structure
Metaphor = direct comparison (no 'like/as') · Simile = comparison WITH 'like/as'
Asyndeton speeds a list; polysyndeton slows it; allusion borrows authority or emotion from a source.

units.name: Style: Diction, Syntax & Tone

concepts.intro: Diction is a writer's specific word choice — and word choice is never neutral; every word carries connotation.
b: Denotation is a word's literal dictionary definition; connotation is the emotional association attached to it.
'Slender' and 'skinny' can denote the same thing but carry very different connotations (positive vs. negative).
Formal diction uses elevated, precise vocabulary; colloquial diction uses casual, everyday language — the choice signals audience and tone.
Concrete diction (specific, sensory) creates vivid images; abstract diction (general, conceptual) creates a more analytical or distanced feel.

concepts.intro: Syntax is how a writer arranges words and constructs sentences — sentence structure itself is a rhetorical choice.
b: Short, simple sentences create emphasis, urgency, or a blunt tone.
Long, complex sentences with multiple clauses can build a sense of accumulation, complexity, or breathless momentum.
A sentence fragment used deliberately can create dramatic emphasis on a single idea.
Sentence variety (mixing short and long sentences) controls pacing and keeps the reader engaged.

concepts.intro: Tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject — and tone can, and often does, shift over the course of a passage.
b: Tone words must be specific and precise: not just 'angry' but 'indignant,' 'contemptuous,' or 'exasperated.'
A tone shift is often signaled by a transition word ('but,' 'however,' 'yet') or a change in sentence structure.
Identifying WHERE a tone shift happens and WHY the writer made that choice is a common analysis task.

concepts.intro: Who is telling the story or making the argument, and how, shapes the entire piece.
b: First person ('I') creates intimacy and personal authority; third person creates distance and can seem more objective.
An author's overall 'voice' — the combination of diction, syntax, and tone that makes their writing recognizable — is called style.
Register refers to how formal or informal the language is relative to the occasion.

concepts.intro: Concrete detail and sensory language work together to shape the reader's experience and judgment.
b: Imagery is language that appeals to the senses; it makes an abstraction vivid and felt.
Selection of detail is itself an argument: what a writer chooses to show reveals a stance.
Figurative diction (metaphor woven into word choice) colors a subject positively or negatively.
Juxtaposing images can imply a comparison or contrast without stating it.
Ask what impression the accumulated details create and why the writer wants it.

concepts.intro: Where a writer places the main clause changes emphasis and suspense.
b: A periodic sentence delays the main idea until the end, building suspense and emphasis.
A cumulative (loose) sentence states the main idea first, then adds modifying detail.
Long, complex sentences can suggest careful reasoning; short sentences land with force.
A single short sentence after several long ones creates emphasis by contrast.
Analyze syntax by describing the pattern and its effect on pace and emphasis.

traps: Using a vague, overused tone word like 'happy' or 'sad' instead of a precise word that matches the passage's actual nuance.
Assuming short sentences always mean 'simple' ideas — short sentences are often used for emphasis on a COMPLEX or weighty idea.
Forgetting that diction and syntax are TOOLS for creating tone — don't discuss them as separate, unconnected observations.
Calling a passage's tone 'negative' or 'positive' instead of naming a precise attitude (wry, indignant, elegiac, admiring).
fms: Denotation = literal meaning · Connotation = emotional association
Short syntax = emphasis/urgency · Long syntax = accumulation/complexity
Tone = the writer's ATTITUDE toward the subject, and it can shift
Periodic sentence delays the main clause for emphasis; cumulative sentence leads with it and adds detail.

units.name: Claims, Evidence & Commentary

concepts.intro: Every argument is built on a claim — but not all claims are the same kind.
b: A claim of fact asserts something is true or false and can be verified.
A claim of value argues something is good, bad, right, or wrong.
A claim of policy argues that something should or should not be done.
A strong thesis usually combines these — it takes a clear, specific, arguable position, not just a statement of topic.

concepts.intro: Evidence is what makes a claim more than just an opinion — different kinds of evidence serve different purposes.
b: Statistical evidence (data, numbers, studies) supports logos-based arguments.
Anecdotal evidence (a specific story or example) supports pathos and makes an abstract point concrete.
Expert testimony borrows credibility (ethos) from an authority on the subject.
Historical or literary evidence draws parallels or precedent to support a claim.

concepts.intro: The single most common weakness in student writing is substituting summary for commentary — commentary is what actually earns credit.
b: Summary restates WHAT the evidence says; commentary explains WHY that evidence matters and HOW it supports the argument.
A good ratio is roughly one sentence of evidence to two or more sentences of commentary/analysis.
Commentary should answer 'so what?' — why does this evidence prove the claim, and why should the reader care?

concepts.intro: A line of reasoning is the logical thread that connects a thesis through each piece of evidence to a coherent overall argument.
b: Each body paragraph should advance a DIFFERENT piece of the argument, not repeat the same point with new evidence.
Reasoning should flow logically: claim → evidence → commentary that connects the evidence back to the claim.
A strong essay's paragraphs build on each other in a deliberate order, not just a random list of separate points.

concepts.intro: Strong arguments limit their claims to what the evidence can actually support.
b: Qualifiers (often, in most cases, under these conditions) make a claim more defensible.
A concession acknowledges a limit or an opposing point without abandoning the thesis.
Overstated claims ('this proves', 'everyone knows') invite easy refutation.
Scope words (all, some, many) should match the strength of the evidence.
On the exam, a qualified, precise thesis usually earns more than a sweeping one.

concepts.intro: Evidence must be both on-point and adequate in amount and kind to support the claim.
b: Relevant evidence bears directly on the specific claim, not a loosely related one.
Sufficient evidence is enough, and varied enough, to make the claim credible.
One vivid anecdote is rarely sufficient for a broad claim.
Cherry-picked data is relevant but insufficient (and misleading).
Evaluate a source by asking: does this actually support the point, and is it enough?

traps: Writing paragraphs that are mostly SUMMARY of the evidence with little or no commentary explaining its significance.
Presenting evidence without ever explicitly connecting it back to the thesis — the reader should never have to guess why a piece of evidence was included.
Repeating the same underlying point in multiple body paragraphs instead of building a genuine line of reasoning.
Summarizing what the evidence says and calling it commentary — commentary explains HOW the evidence proves the claim.
fms: Claim types: fact, value, policy
Summary = restates WHAT evidence says · Commentary = explains WHY it matters
Line of reasoning = claim → evidence → commentary, building logically paragraph to paragraph
Good evidence is relevant AND sufficient; a qualifier narrows a claim to what the evidence supports.

units.name: Organization, Structure & Counterargument

concepts.intro: A strong introduction orients the reader and stakes out a clear, defensible position.
b: An effective thesis is specific and arguable — someone could reasonably disagree with it.
Avoid a thesis that simply restates the prompt or announces intent ('In this essay I will discuss...').
The introduction should establish context briefly before arriving at the thesis — it doesn't need to be long.

concepts.intro: Each body paragraph should function as a self-contained argument that supports the overall thesis.
b: A topic sentence should state the paragraph's specific claim, not just announce a topic.
Evidence should be integrated smoothly, not simply dropped in as an unexplained quotation.
Commentary should close the paragraph by tying the evidence explicitly back to the thesis.

concepts.intro: Addressing the other side of an argument — rather than ignoring it — actually strengthens a writer's credibility and position.
b: A concession acknowledges a valid point on the opposing side before pivoting back to your own argument.
A rebuttal directly refutes an opposing point, explaining why it's flawed or less compelling.
Ignoring the strongest counterarguments makes an essay seem one-sided or naive, weakening ethos.

concepts.intro: Transitions and conclusions are what make an essay feel unified rather than like a list of disconnected paragraphs.
b: Transitions should show the LOGICAL relationship between ideas (contrast, cause-effect, addition), not just be a filler word.
An effective conclusion does more than restate the thesis — it can broaden the argument's significance or implications.
A conclusion that introduces a brand-new, unsupported argument is a structural weakness, not a strength.

concepts.intro: Writers organize material in patterns that fit their purpose.
b: Chronological / narrative order suits process, history, or personal experience.
Cause and effect traces why something happened or what it will produce.
Problem-solution names a problem, then argues for a response.
Comparison-contrast sets two things side by side to clarify or evaluate.
Order of importance (climactic) builds to the strongest point.

concepts.intro: Well-organized prose guides the reader from one idea to the next without gaps.
b: The 'given-new' principle: start sentences with familiar information, end with the new point.
Repeating key terms (rather than elegant variation) keeps a thread visible.
Pointing words (this, that, such, these) must have a clear referent.
Transitions should name the logical relationship (however, therefore, for instance), not just decorate.
Paragraph breaks signal a shift in subtopic or stage of the argument.

traps: Writing a thesis that is simply a factual statement or announces the essay's topic instead of taking an arguable position.
Including a counterargument only to dismiss it in one weak sentence instead of genuinely engaging with and rebutting it.
Using transition words ('also,' 'another thing') that show ADDITION but not actual logical relationship between ideas.
Using transition words that mislabel the relationship (writing 'however' where there is no contrast).
fms: Effective thesis = specific + arguable, not just a topic announcement
Concession = acknowledge opposing point · Rebuttal = explain why it's less compelling
Transitions should show logical relationship, not just list ideas
Given-new: open with the known, close with the new; transitions must name the logical relationship.

units.name: The Synthesis Essay

concepts.intro: The synthesis essay asks you to develop your OWN argument on a topic, using multiple provided sources as support.
b: You must take and defend a clear position on the prompt's issue — the sources are tools for YOUR argument, not the point of the essay.
You must cite at least three of the provided sources to support your line of reasoning.
The essay is not a summary of what each source says — that earns little credit on its own.

concepts.intro: Choosing which sources to use — and how to use them — is a strategic part of the synthesis essay.
b: Pick sources that best support the specific argument you're making, not just the first three in the packet.
You can use a source to support your point, or strategically use one to acknowledge and rebut a counterargument.
Cite sources by their letter (e.g., 'Source B') or a clear paraphrase — don't just quote at length without analysis.

concepts.intro: The most common way to lose points on the synthesis essay is turning it into a source-by-source book report.
b: Never organize the essay source-by-source ('Source A says... Source B says...') — organize it by YOUR own points, drawing on sources as needed within each.
Every citation needs commentary explaining how it supports YOUR specific claim.
A strong synthesis essay could be outlined using only the writer's own claims — the sources fill in the support.

concepts.intro: Because the synthesis prompt is often a genuinely debatable issue, a defensible, specific position is essential.
b: A qualified position (agreeing with conditions or nuance) is completely acceptable and often stronger than an all-or-nothing stance.
Avoid a wishy-washy thesis that doesn't actually commit to anything — pick a specific, defensible lane.
Anticipate the strongest counterargument to your position and address it using one of the sources.

concepts.intro: The synthesis essay asks you to build your own argument using sources, not to report on them.
b: Summary reports what each source says; synthesis uses sources as evidence for your claims.
Compare-contrast weighs sources against each other; synthesis subordinates them to your line of reasoning.
Organize body paragraphs around your sub-claims, bringing in whichever sources support each.
Sources that disagree are useful: use one to complicate or answer another.
Every citation should be doing a job in your argument.

concepts.intro: Sources must be integrated smoothly and credited clearly.
b: A signal phrase names the source in the sentence ('Source A argues that ...').
A parenthetical citation places the reference at the end ((Source A)).
Quote sparingly and only when the wording matters; otherwise paraphrase.
Introduce a quotation; never drop it in without framing.
The AP synthesis prompt requires citing at least three of the provided sources.

traps: Summarizing each source in order instead of organizing the essay around your OWN claims with sources woven in as support.
Using fewer than three sources, or using sources without explaining how they support your specific argument.
Writing a thesis so vague or two-sided that it doesn't actually take a defensible position.
Walking through the sources one by one (Source A says..., Source B says...) instead of organizing by your own claims.
fms: Minimum 3 sources cited, used to support YOUR argument (not summarized in order)
Organize by YOUR claims, not source-by-source
A qualified, specific thesis beats a vague, all-sides-equally thesis
Synthesis organizes by YOUR claims; cite at least three sources; signal phrase names the source in the sentence.

units.name: The Rhetorical Analysis Essay

concepts.intro: This essay asks you to explain HOW a writer builds their argument, not whether you agree with it.
b: You are analyzing the WRITER'S choices (rhetorical strategies) and their effect on the intended audience — not arguing the topic yourself.
Start by identifying the rhetorical situation: speaker, audience, purpose, occasion.
A strong thesis identifies the writer's overall purpose AND previews the strategies you'll analyze to achieve it.

concepts.intro: You can't analyze everything in a passage — choosing a few strong, well-supported strategies is more effective than a shallow list.
b: Choose 2–3 rhetorical strategies (appeals, devices, structure, diction/syntax) that are clearly present and significant.
Pick strategies you can trace across MULTIPLE parts of the passage, not just a single isolated line.
Organize by strategy or by the passage's structure (chronological) — either is valid if the reasoning is clear.

concepts.intro: The core skill of rhetorical analysis is always the same move: identify a specific choice, then explain its effect on the audience.
b: Never just quote a line and label a device — always follow with 'this creates the effect of...' or 'this persuades the audience to...'
Effects should tie back to the writer's overall purpose established in your thesis.
Strong analysis explains WHY a specific word or structure was chosen over alternatives, not just that it exists.

concepts.intro: There's no single required structure, but successful essays usually follow one of two reliable patterns.
b: Strategy-based structure: one body paragraph per rhetorical strategy, tracing it through the whole passage.
Chronological structure: body paragraphs follow the passage's own organization (beginning, middle, end), analyzing shifts in strategy along the way.
Whichever structure you choose, each paragraph needs its own clear claim about a specific strategy's effect.

concepts.intro: A rhetorical analysis thesis makes a defensible claim about the writer's choices and their purpose.
b: A weak thesis lists devices ('the author uses ethos, pathos, and logos').
A strong thesis states what the writer is doing and to what end ('to build urgency, the writer...').
It should be arguable: someone could reasonably read the choices differently.
It previews a line of reasoning, not a checklist.
The body then shows HOW specific choices create the effect the thesis names.

concepts.intro: Tone is the writer's attitude; changes in tone are deliberate and meaningful.
b: Name tone precisely (measured, scornful, wistful, urgent), not just 'serious' or 'emotional'.
Diction, syntax, imagery, and figurative language together create tone.
A shift in tone (marked by 'but', a new paragraph, a change in sentence length) signals a turn in the argument.
Explain what the shift accomplishes for the writer's purpose.
Track tone across the passage rather than assigning one label to the whole.

traps: Arguing FOR OR AGAINST the passage's topic instead of analyzing HOW the writer builds their argument — this is the single most common rhetorical analysis error.
Quote-dropping: including a quotation from the passage without explaining the specific effect it creates.
Choosing too many strategies to discuss shallowly instead of a few strategies discussed in real depth.
Device-dropping: naming a strategy and quoting a line without explaining the effect on the audience.
fms: Rhetorical analysis = HOW the writer argues, not whether you agree
Always follow device identification with its EFFECT on the audience
2–3 well-developed strategies beat 5+ shallow ones
Analytical thesis = what the writer does + to what end; a tonal shift marks a turn in the argument.

units.name: The Argument Essay

concepts.intro: The argument essay gives you a general claim or issue and asks YOU to develop and defend your own position using evidence from your own knowledge.
b: Unlike synthesis, there are no provided sources — evidence comes from your own reading, knowledge, and experience.
You may agree, disagree, or agree with qualifications — any defensible position is acceptable if well-supported.
The evidence you choose should be specific and relevant, not vague generalities.

concepts.intro: Specific, well-explained evidence is far more persuasive than a long list of vague examples.
b: Historical examples, current events, literature, and personal experience are all valid evidence sources.
One or two well-developed examples with real commentary beat five examples mentioned in passing.
Evidence should be verifiably true or at least reasonably plausible — invented 'facts' undermine credibility.

concepts.intro: A clear structure with acknowledged complexity signals sophisticated, college-level thinking.
b: State a clear, specific, defensible thesis early — avoid restating the prompt as your thesis.
Address a counterargument to show you've considered the issue's complexity, then explain why your position still holds.
A qualified thesis ('X is true, except when...') often demonstrates more sophisticated thinking than an absolute claim.

concepts.intro: The highest-scoring argument essays go beyond a basic thesis-evidence-conclusion structure to show real intellectual engagement.
b: Explaining the broader implications or stakes of your argument demonstrates sophistication.
Making nuanced distinctions (this is true in some contexts but not others) shows sophistication over an all-or-nothing stance.
A vivid, effective writing style alone does not equal sophistication — it must be paired with genuinely complex reasoning.

concepts.l: Line of reasoning, refutation, and concession
concepts.intro: An argument essay needs a clear through-line and an honest treatment of opposing views.
b: The line of reasoning is the logical sequence connecting thesis, sub-claims, and evidence.
Refutation directly answers an opposing argument and shows why it fails.
Concession grants that an opposing point has some merit, then limits its importance.
Concede-then-counter ('while X is true, it does not follow that Y') strengthens ethos.
Every body paragraph should visibly advance the thesis.

concepts.intro: The highest scores reward complexity, not just competence.
b: Sophistication can come from situating the argument in a broader context.
It can come from acknowledging tensions or complications in your own position.
A qualified, nuanced claim ('this holds in most cases, but...') often reads as more sophisticated.
Vivid, purposeful style contributes to the impression of sophistication.
End by answering 'so what?' — why the argument matters.

traps: Restating the prompt itself as your thesis instead of taking your own specific, arguable position.
Using vague, unverifiable 'evidence' ('studies show...') without any specific, concrete example.
Ignoring the counterargument entirely, which makes the essay's reasoning seem incomplete or naive.
Listing many shallow examples; two well-developed examples that are analyzed usually score higher.
fms: Argument essay = YOUR position, YOUR evidence (no provided sources)
1-2 well-developed examples beat 5 shallow ones
Sophistication = nuance and qualification, not just vivid language
Concede-then-counter to build ethos; sophistication = nuance, context, and answering 'so what?'.

units.name: Grammar, Conventions & Multiple-Choice Strategy

concepts.intro: The multiple-choice section tests your ability to spot and fix grammar and structure problems in real writing.
b: A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma — fix with a period, semicolon, or coordinating conjunction.
A sentence fragment is missing a subject, verb, or complete thought and cannot stand alone.
A run-on sentence joins independent clauses with no punctuation or connector at all.

concepts.intro: Consistency in grammatical form is tested constantly — mismatched structures are one of the most common 'fix this' question types.
b: Items in a list or series must share the same grammatical form ('to run, to jump, and to swim' — not 'to run, jumping, and swim').
Subject-verb agreement: a singular subject takes a singular verb, even when other words come between them.
Pronoun-antecedent agreement: a pronoun must match its antecedent in number ('everyone' is singular, so it takes 'his or her,' not 'their' in the strictest formal usage tested).

concepts.intro: Reading-based multiple choice questions test close reading of nonfiction passages, similar to the skills used in rhetorical analysis.
b: Questions ask you to identify a passage's main claim, a specific rhetorical strategy's function, or how a paragraph relates to the whole.
Always go back to the passage to verify an answer choice rather than relying on memory or general impression.
Wrong answer choices are often 'half-right' — true in general but not actually supported by THIS specific passage.

concepts.intro: Writing-based multiple choice questions ask you to improve a student-written passage, testing revision skills directly.
b: Questions may ask you to choose the best transition, the most effective word choice, or where to place a sentence for better organization.
'Which choice best maintains the tone established in the passage?' questions require checking the surrounding sentences' tone, not just grammar.
Some questions ask which revision would be LEAST effective or should be deleted — read the question direction carefully before answering.

concepts.intro: Beyond correctness, punctuation shapes emphasis and rhythm.
b: A colon introduces an explanation, list, or appositive that completes the preceding clause.
A dash sets off an interruption or emphatic addition, more informal than parentheses.
A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.
Overusing dashes weakens their emphatic force.
On MC 'writing' questions, choose the punctuation that best serves clarity and the intended emphasis.

concepts.intro: Multiple-choice writing questions and your essays reward economical, exact language.
b: Cut redundancy ('past history', 'end result', 'in order to' when 'to' works).
Replace vague words ('things', 'stuff', 'a lot') with specific nouns.
Prefer active voice unless the actor is unknown or unimportant.
Remove filler ('it is important to note that', 'the fact that').
In an MC revision item, the best answer is usually the clearest, not the longest.

traps: Missing that a question asks for the LEAST effective option or which sentence should be DELETED — always read the question stem carefully.
Choosing an answer that is grammatically correct but doesn't match the passage's established tone or purpose.
Fixing a comma splice by just removing the comma entirely, which creates a run-on instead of a correct sentence.
On MC questions, picking the most elaborate or formal-sounding option instead of the clearest and most concise.
fms: Comma splice: two independent clauses joined by ONLY a comma — needs period, semicolon, or conjunction
Parallel structure: matching items must share the same grammatical form
Always verify MC answers against the actual passage text, not general impression
Colon = the clause before it is complete; semicolon joins two independent clauses; cut redundancy and filler.

units.name: GrAmSS

concepts.l: Exam snapshot: what is on Tuesday 10/6
concepts.intro: The Unit 1 Exam covers Great American Short Stories, the Literary Devices packet, the nonfiction sources and every handout from weeks 1-5.
b: Fair game: every story and nonfiction piece in Great American Short Stories (GrAmSS), "The Eve of St. Agnes", Washington Irving / Romanticism, the Emerson handout, and the Literary Devices packet.

The reading list for Unit 1: "Rip Van Winkle", "The Eve of St. Agnes" (Keats), "The Fall of the House of Usher" with its Day 1 and Day 2 handouts (including "The Haunted Palace"), "Baker's Bluejay Yarn", and "Young Goodman Brown".
The only Hawthorne on this exam is "Young Goodman Brown". "The Custom House" and The Scarlet Letter are NOT on this test; they belong to the Unit 2 exam.
The class schedule says you must know every device in the Literary Devices packet: names, definitions and recognizing them in use.

The class schedule does not list the exam format, so prepare to answer analysis questions with evidence (how does the author use a device to convey a purpose?) as well as recognition questions on stories, authors and devices.

Your teacher's go-to question types: open-ended class questions rephrased as multiple choice; which devices are present; the word/line ___ most closely means; vocabulary word to definition; identify the speaker or the person spoken to; what a pronoun refers to; best interpretation of a quote; what the speaker would agree or disagree with; all true/false EXCEPT; chronology; accuracy of events; reading comprehension; interpret/apply; plot recall; historical context.

concepts.l: Introduction to Great American Short Stories (Stegner)
concepts.intro: The class schedule tells you to read the Introduction and connect its definitions to each story and nonfiction piece. It was written by Wallace and Mary Stegner (the anthology is dated 1957); know its main claims.
b: Poe published "Metzengerstein" in the Philadelphia Saturday Courier on January 14, 1832, using for the first time the technique of the single effect on which the modern short story is built. The short story is called an American invention and specialty; Poe and Hawthorne "together created the short story as a form".

Irving vs. Poe: "Rip Van Winkle" is an example of the orderly tale of linked incidents chronologically treated, graceful, humorous and urbane. Poe substituted the concentrated tale of effect: one preconceived impression, action focused on the climactic moment, mood controlled from first to last, improbabilities made plausible by concreteness.

The editors call Poe's terror "not of Germany but of the soul" (Poe's own phrase) yet judge his effects closer to "gooseflesh", and say his "madness" is more literary than observed. They name "The Fall of the House of Usher" Poe at his best, with its doomed mansion and the "deadly inverted image of the fateful house reflected in the tarn". Poe also fathered the tale of ratiocination, the parent of the detective story.

Hawthorne added moral or intellectual weight, Henry Seidel Canby's "specific gravity". The typical American story asks to be taken seriously as a reflection of life, manners, morals or national character. Hawthorne's contribution is the story that probes a situation rather than linking incidents or contriving effects.

Usher and "Young Goodman Brown" are both built on a journey and a return, moving from light into darkness and back to light. Poe's darkness is the theatrical dark of the horror tale; Hawthorne's is the darkness of the soul, the forest of sin. Brown's initiation shows "conviction that virtue is a mask and all men are guilty".

Twain: the Introduction says he never wrote a good short story; his mastered forms were the humorous frontier sketch (his essay "How to Tell a Story") and the fable. "Bluejay Yarn" is not a short story by Matthews' definition but superb in its kind, linked to Harris's Uncle Remus stories and, later, Thurber's fables. The beast story is among the oldest forms of fiction.

Irving's "Rip Van Winkle" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow" are named as his best and best known. The editors' criteria for selection were the excellence of each story in itself and its representativeness in the story's development in the United States.

Later sections trace local color (Bret Harte's "The Luck of Roaring Camp", 1868), Henry James, Stephen Crane, Sherwood Anderson, Hemingway and Faulkner. Only the material connected to your six texts is likely to be tested, but the local-color and beast-fable paragraphs support Twain.

concepts.intro: Romanticism is the frame for the whole unit. Irving's packet content is on the exam, so know the movement's vocabulary as well as the man.
b: Romanticism (late 18th to mid 19th century, per the Britannica handout) rejects the order, calm, harmony, balance and rationality of Classicism and late-18th-century Neoclassicism, and reacts against the Enlightenment, rationalism and physical materialism.

Romanticism emphasizes the individual, the subjective, the irrational, the imaginative, the emotional and the transcendental; it loves nature, exalts emotion over reason and the senses over intellect, and has a predilection for the exotic, mysterious, occult, monstrous and even satanic.
Classicism and Neoclassicism prized order, reason and restraint; Rationalism trusted reason above feeling. Romantic writers push back with intuition, mystery and the sublime.
Washington Irving (1783-1859) is often called the first American author to win international fame. "Rip Van Winkle" appeared in The Sketch Book (1819-20) under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon.
Irving frames the tale as papers left by the fictional historian Diedrich Knickerbocker, a playful fake-history frame (historiography: how history gets written).
Romantic markers to spot in the stories: dreamlike or supernatural events, wild nature, nostalgia for the past, a lone individual against society, and strong emotion.
Packet vocabulary to know: Classicism, Neoclassicism, Enlightenment, Rationalism, Transcendental, exaltation, predilection, occult, satanic, historiography.

English Romanticism began in the 1790s with Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads; Wordsworth's 1800 Preface called poetry "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings". Blake was a third early poet; Keats, Byron and Shelley are the later high point; Scott is credited with the historical novel.

Gothic fiction combines horror and romance. Its origin is credited to Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1764, subtitled "A Gothic Story"); later examples include Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, Poe, and Stoker's Dracula. "Gothic" refers to the pseudo-medieval buildings where many of the stories take place.

concepts.intro: Class aim: How does Washington Irving use characterization to develop a central idea and his purpose? Setting, mood and the time period do a lot of the work.
b: Setting (pp. 33-34): the Kaatskill Mountains and a Dutch village founded in the time of Peter Stuyvesant, "while the country was yet a province of Great Britain". The village inn is marked by a portrait of King George the Third. Rip falls asleep under British rule and wakes to a United States.

Characterization of Rip (pp. 34-36): "a simple, good-natured fellow", "a kind neighbor and an obedient henpecked husband", beloved by wives, children and dogs; his "great error" is "an insuperable aversion to all kinds of profitable labor", though he will help any neighbor. His farm is "the most pestilent little piece of ground", his patrimonial estate dwindles, and his son Rip is a ragged "urchin".

Dame Van Winkle (pp. 34, 36-38): a "termagant" and "virago" whose tongue is "the only edged tool that grows keener with constant use". Irving jokes that henpecking makes men "obsequious and conciliating abroad". The women of the village side with Rip. Irving's language clearly favors Rip, which the class schedule asks you to examine (males vs. females; pathos).

Rip's club (pp. 37-38): idle men on a bench before the inn under the King George portrait, a "junto" controlled by the silent landlord Nicholas Vedder, with the schoolmaster Derrick Van Brummel reading old newspapers. Irving pokes fun at slow village politics.

The mountain (pp. 38-42): a voice calls "Rip Van Winkle!"; Wolf bristles; a short, square-built man in antique Dutch dress carries a keg; they climb to a hollow where silent, gloomy men play ninepins and the balls echo like thunder; Rip drinks from the flagons and falls into a deep sleep.
Waking (pp. 42-43): a rusty firelock, a beard a foot long, no Wolf, and a village where people stroke their chins at him, dogs bark, and houses have changed. His own house is decayed and empty.

The changed inn (pp. 44-47): "The Union Hotel, by Jonathan Doolittle", a pole with a flag of stars and stripes, and the sign changed from the red coat and King to "GENERAL WASHINGTON". A bustling, disputatious crowd argues about rights, elections, Congress, liberty and Bunker's Hill. Rip is asked whether he is Federal or Democrat, says he is "a loyal subject of the King", and is called a Tory.

Identity (pp. 47-49): Nicholas Vedder is dead 18 years; Brom Dutcher died at Stony Point; Van Brummel is in Congress. Rip cries "Does nobody here know Rip Van Winkle?" and sees his lazy double, young Rip. He says he is his daughter Judith Gardenier's father; an old woman recognizes him; Peter Vanderdonk confirms the legend of Hendrick Hudson's crew of the Halfmoon, who visit the mountains every twenty years.

Ending (pp. 49-51): Rip lives with Judith, resumes idleness, and becomes a patriarch and chronicler of "the old times before the war". Irving notes he escaped one despotism, "petticoat government", and that henpecked husbands still wish for "a quieting draught out of Rip Van Winkle's flagon". The Note claims the tale may derive from a German legend (Emperor Frederick der Rothbart) but that Knickerbocker swears it is fact.
Big ideas: change vs. tradition, freedom vs. duty, and the new American identity; also Romantic elements (mountains, supernatural, nostalgia) and Irving's humor and irony.

concepts.intro: Class aim: How can we better understand what we read by researching vocabulary and identifying literary devices? This is a long narrative poem (42 stanzas), so know the story and the devices.
b: John Keats (1795-1821) wrote it in 1819; it was published in 1820. It is a Romantic narrative poem in Spenserian stanzas (nine lines, rhyme ABABBCBCC, last line longer).
The legend: on St. Agnes' Eve (January 20), a young woman who follows certain rituals may dream of her future husband. Madeline tries this.

Story: Porphyro, from a family hostile to Madeline's, sneaks in with the help of the old nurse Angela, prepares a feast, and wakes Madeline from her dream. They flee into the storm. At the end, the Beadsman and Angela die.

Devices to label in your stanzas: rich sensory imagery, alliteration, personification, contrast (cold outside vs. warm inside, holy vs. sensual), allusion (Romeo-and-Juliet-style feuding families), and setting/mood.
Framing: the poem opens in bitter cold and ends with a cold death, which sets a wistful, fragile mood around the lovers' warmth. Be ready to say what message you think Keats sends and how you know.
Cross-connection: the class schedule asks you to compare it with "The Fall of the House of Usher" and "The Haunted Palace" (romance, dreams, and the fall of a great house).

Opening: "St. Agnes' Eve - Ah, bitter chill it was! The owl, for all his feathers, was a-cold"; the Beadsman's frosted breath rises "like pious incense". Angela warns Porphyro that the Baron's household is hostile ("He curs'd thee and thine, both house and land"). Porphyro sets a feast and plays an ancient ditty on Madeline's lute; when she wakes he says "Awake! arise! my love", and they flee "into the storm".

concepts.l: "The Fall of the House of Usher" (Poe, 1839)
concepts.intro: Class aim: How does Poe's use of language (literary and rhetorical devices) convey his message? Group work covered Roderick, Madeline and the house.
b: Gothic short story: an unnamed narrator answers a letter from his boyhood friend Roderick Usher, who is ill in mind and body, and stays at the gloomy family mansion.

Setting and imagery: a dull, dark, soundless autumn day; low clouds; "vacant eye-like windows" and decayed trees. The words create dread and gloom (mood). The house is nearly a character (personification).

Roderick: hypersensitive to light, sound and touch, nervous and doomed. Madeline: his twin, wasting from a strange illness. Poe's characterization is mostly indirect (through appearance, behavior and speech).
Madeline is entombed in the house while seemingly dead; later she appears, and Roderick dies of terror. The house cracks along a fissure and falls into the tarn.
"The Haunted Palace" is a poem inside the story: a fair palace ruled by Thought falls to "evil things", mirroring Roderick's mind and the house's fate (allegory / mirror image).
The "Mad Trist" (the hero is Ethelred) that the narrator reads aloud echoes real sounds in the house. Poe's inserted texts create foreshadowing and blur fiction and reality.
Poe's goal is a single, unified effect: dread. Ask for each detail: what feeling does this word choice create?

Class pages: Roderick (70-71, 74), Madeline (77, 90), the house (72-73, 91); "The Haunted Palace" (79-81); the Ethelred excerpts (87-89). Handout vocab from the poem: seraph, pinion (wing), ramparts, discordant, throng, lute.

Class questions: To what extent is the house a character? For what reasons does Roderick prematurely entomb Madeline? Why might Poe write so graphically and gothically? How does Poe use ethos, logos and pathos, and elevated vocabulary?

concepts.intro: Class aim: In what ways does Twain use literary devices (anthropomorphism, characterization, point of view, metaphor) to advance the theme? A tall tale told in a folksy voice.
b: Mark Twain (1835-1910) wrote it in 1880 (from A Tramp Abroad). A yarn is a tale of adventure or incredible happenings, often exaggerated.

Baker's claims about jays: more moods and feelings than other creatures; "book-talk" "bristling with metaphor"; better grammar than a cat; "more principle than a Congressman" (none); they lie, steal, deceive, betray and "outswear any gentleman in the mines"; a jay can "cry", "laugh", "feel shame", "reason and plan and discuss", likes gossip and has "a sense of humor". "If a jay ain't human, he better take in his sign."

Twain frames the tale: "Animals talk to each other, of course," and he knew one man who understood them, Jim Baker, a middle-aged, simple-hearted California miner. Baker says bluejays are the best talkers of all birds and beasts, with more moods than other creatures, good grammar, metaphor, and the ability to outswear a miner.

The centerpiece (pp. 138-141): Baker says the last neighbor left seven years ago and his log house, one big room with a plank roof and no ceiling, has been empty. A jay finds a knot-hole in the roof, exclaims "it's a perfectly elegant hole!", drops an acorn, and does not hear it fall. He drops more, grows furious, swears "cussed himself black in the face", works for about two and a half hours, and says he has put in "not any less than two tons".

Other jays come, then "five thousand", each offering a "leather-headed" opinion, until an old jay lands on the half-open door and sees the acorns scattered across the floor: "hang'd if this fool hasn't been trying to fill up a house with acorns!" The jays fall over "suffocating with laughter"; jays came every summer for three years; only an owl from Nova Scotia, visiting Yosemite, saw nothing funny.
Anthropomorphism: giving animate beings (animals) human traits. Personification: giving inanimate objects human traits. The jays act like people, and that is the joke and the point.

Point of view: the story is told through Baker's own dialect-rich voice inside Twain's frame. Twain indirectly characterizes Baker (folksy, sincere, observant, prone to exaggeration) through his speech.
Juxtaposition: putting things side by side for effect. Twain sets Baker's serious, respectful tone against a ridiculous story, which creates the humor and irony.

Theme prompt from class: the jay and the knothole may work as a metaphor for human existence (a foolish, futile effort that others laugh at when they see the whole picture). Also connect it to Twain's era: he lived 1835-1910 and the story was written in 1880.
Rhetorical view: ask what Twain's intent is in telling this story, and how humor, dialect and hyperbole build ethos with the reader.

concepts.intro: Class aim: In what ways is Hawthorne's use of setting, characterization, allusion and foreshadowing significant? This is the only Hawthorne work on the exam.
b: Setting: Salem Village, Massachusetts, in Puritan times. Brown leaves his wife Faith at sunset for an "errand" in the dark forest.

The traveler (about fifty and resembling Brown) has a staff like a great black snake that seems to "twist and wriggle itself like a living serpent" (an allusion to Eden). He claims to have helped Brown's grandfather, the constable, lash a Quaker woman through Salem, and Brown's father burn an Indian village in King Philip's war; he says deacons, selectmen and the Great and General Court are his supporters.

On the path Brown sees Goody Cloyse, who taught him his catechism and greets the traveler as "your worship"; he hears (but cannot see) the minister and Deacon Gookin riding to the meeting; a cloud carries voices including Faith's, and a pink ribbon falls. Brown cries "My Faith is gone!" and rushes to the forest meeting, a blazing altar-rock, where he sees the minister, Gookin, Goody Cloyse and Martha Carrier (a real Salem-trial name) among the congregation.

The dark figure, in the shape of a grave divine, says "Welcome, my children, to the communion of your race" and "Evil is the nature of mankind". Brown, about to be baptized in the blood-like basin, cries "Faith! Faith! look up to heaven, and resist the wicked one" and suddenly finds himself alone in the calm night.

Next morning the minister, Deacon Gookin praying, Goody Cloyse catechizing a girl, and Faith with her pink ribbons all appear normal; Brown shuns them. Hawthorne asks, "Had Goodman Brown fallen asleep in the forest and only dreamed a wild dream of a witch-meeting? Be it so if you will".
Symbols and allegory: Faith (his wife and his religious faith), the pink ribbons (innocence), the forest (moral wilderness and the unknown), the serpent staff (evil). Names carry meaning.
Ambiguity: Brown wakes in the morning. Was it a dream or reality? Hawthorne never tells you. What matters is that Brown returns changed.
Ending: Brown sees hypocrisy in everyone and lives "a stern, a sad, a darkly meditative" man who is distrustful; his death is unmarked by hope. His faith in people is destroyed.

Hawthorne's attitude: a critical view of Puritan rigidity, hypocrisy and the idea that everyone is secretly sinful. Hawthorne's own ancestors took part in the Salem witch trials, which colors the tone.

Allusions to the Bible (the serpent, Satan, the devil's prayers, baptism and communion parodies) are central. Say why Hawthorne uses allusion: it deepens the moral stakes for readers who recognize the source.

Class questions: how the settings, direct/indirect characterization of Brown and his companion, and the Biblical allusions work; what Hawthorne feels about Puritans; and the take-away or thesis he intends.

Key lines to know: Faith "thrust her own pretty head into the street, letting the wind play with the pink ribbons of her cap"; "My Faith is gone! ... There is no good on earth; and sin is but a name. Come, devil! for to thee is this world given"; "Faith! Faith! look up to Heaven, and resist the Wicked One!"; "his dying hour was gloom".

concepts.intro: The Emerson handout (Lesson #5) is an excerpt from "The Transcendentalist". Class question: how does it reflect themes from the Great American Short Stories unit? Bullet-point summary of the argument is on your notes.
b: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803-1882) was the leading voice of American Transcendentalism, a Romantic movement that trusts intuition, individual conscience and nature over institutions and tradition.

From the excerpt: the materialist "takes his departure from the external world" and esteems a man as one product of it, respecting society, government, social art, luxury and "every mass". The idealist "takes his departure from his consciousness, and reckons the world an appearance".

The idealist's measure is metaphysical: the rank things take in his consciousness, not their size or appearance. "Mind is the only reality, of which men and all other natures are better or worse reflectors." Nature, literature and history are "subjective phenomena".

The idealist does not respect government, church, charities, property or the arts for themselves, only as symbols of the laws of being, and sees facts flowing outward "from an invisible, unsounded centre in himself". His thought "is the Universe".
Use the handout: quote how Emerson defines each side, then say what he means and how you know from his diction.
Connect to the unit: Rip resists social duties (individual vs. society); Goodman Brown loses faith in his community; Poe's Roderick lives inside his own mind; Keats prizes imagination.
Emerson is nonfiction (an essay/lecture), so you can also discuss purpose, audience, tone and ethos, logos and pathos in it.
The class schedule also asks you to connect each definition on the Introduction to Great American Short Stories to each story you read.

concepts.intro: Grade 11 essential question: How can we critically interpret the American Dream? The class schedule had you deconstruct James Truslow Adams' definition.
b: James Truslow Adams popularized the phrase in The Epic of America (1931): a dream of a land where life is better, richer and fuller for everyone, with opportunity for each person according to ability or achievement.

Adams stresses that it is not just cars and high wages but a social order where each person can reach their fullest stature. Notice how diction like "better and richer and fuller" makes it about more than money.

Handout details: Adams wrote it in The Epic of America (1931, pp. 214-215); the dream is "for the European upper classes" hard to interpret, many Americans had "grown weary and mistrustful of it", and each person should be "recognized by others for what they are, regardless of the fortuitous circumstances of birth or position".

The handout also quotes the Declaration of Independence (life, Liberty and the Pursuit of Happiness), asks whether homesteaders, immigrants and World War II veterans pursued the same dream, and notes critics who say it became material prosperity or is out of reach for the working poor. Thomas Wolfe is quoted on "his shining, golden opportunity".
Ask of each story: whose version of the dream is shown, and who is left out or disillusioned?

Rip Van Winkle: freedom from duty and the birth of a new nation. Goodman Brown: the Puritan ideal of a godly community, undone by hypocrisy. Baker's yarn: folksy Western tall tale that pokes fun at human effort.
The class prompt for the summer reading response asked: In what ways did the text portray the author's notion of the American Dream? Use the same question with any of these stories.
Definition is a moving target: consider how the dream has evolved and what it is not.

concepts.intro: You must know every device in your Literary Devices packet (names, definitions, recognizing usage). This is the working set for Unit 1; confirm each definition in your packet.
b: Imagery: language that appeals to the senses. Mood: the feeling created for the reader. Tone: the author's attitude toward the subject.
Setting: time and place. Characterization: how the author creates people: direct (the narrator tells you) vs. indirect (speech, actions, thoughts, appearance, others' reactions).
Point of view: who narrates (first person, third limited, omniscient). A frame narrative is a story that holds another story.
Allusion: an indirect reference to a person, place, text or idea of cultural, literary, historical or political significance. Foreshadowing: hints about what comes next.
Symbolism: an object, character or action that stands for a bigger idea. Allegory: a story where characters and events symbolize a moral or political meaning throughout.
Irony (situational, verbal, dramatic), juxtaposition, metaphor, simile, hyperbole, personification vs. anthropomorphism, diction (word choice), syntax (sentence structure).
Rhetorical appeals: ethos (credibility), logos (logic), pathos (emotion). Apply them to the authors' language, not just to essays.

concepts.l: How to write and answer analysis questions
concepts.intro: The class schedule trains a specific answer style; use it on the exam. "Aim" questions usually ask how an author uses a device to convey a message.
b: Use direct text evidence and cite it (author, title, page or line). Explain how the exact words create the effect.
For multi-part questions, write ONE cohesive response that covers every part, using transitions to link them to your claim.
Effective paragraph basic structure: claim, evidence, commentary, and a link back to the claim. Use the template on the Effective Paragraph handout for multiple quotes.
Mood-of-the-text (MOT) routine: underline evidence, circle the key word that creates the feeling, label the mood, then explain how the words work together.
Pivotal questions are open-ended and text-based, not hunt-and-fetch: To what extent... In what ways... For what reasons... How is/does... and why is it significant?
SOAPSTone (Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone) works on fiction and nonfiction; state purpose as a verb phrase (to warn, to satirize, to mourn).

concepts.l: Authors, dates and forms cheat sheet
concepts.intro: A fast-recall table for the recognition questions. Dates are the standard publication years; check any date on your packet.
b: Irving (1783-1859): "Rip Van Winkle" (The Sketch Book, 1819-20). Romantic, satirical, folk-legend tone.
Keats (1795-1821): "The Eve of St. Agnes" (written 1819, published 1820). Narrative poem, Spenserian stanza.
Poe (1809-1849): "The Fall of the House of Usher" (1839). Gothic; contains "The Haunted Palace" and the "Mad Trist" of Ethelred.
Twain (1835-1910): "Baker's Bluejay Yarn" (1880). Humorous frame plus tall tale; anthropomorphism and dialect.
Hawthorne (1804-1864): "Young Goodman Brown" (1835). Dark Romanticism / Puritan allegory.
Emerson (1803-1882): "The Transcendentalist" (essay/lecture). Nonfiction; idealism vs. materialism.

concepts.intro: The Irving handout is a Wikipedia biography with discussion questions. Expect accuracy-of-information and historical-context questions from it.
b: Washington Irving (April 3, 1783 - November 28, 1859) was born in Manhattan the same week New Yorkers learned of the British ceasefire that ended the Revolution. His mother named him for George Washington, whom he met at age six.

Boyhood trips up the Hudson, including the Catskill region (the setting of "Rip Van Winkle"), shaped him: he wrote that the Kaatskill Mountains had "the most witching effect on my boyish imagination". Tarrytown gave him Sleepy Hollow's Dutch customs and ghost stories.

Early writing: letters to the Morning Chronicle (1802) as Jonathan Oldstyle; the magazine Salmagundi (1807), which nicknamed New York "Gotham"; then A History of New-York by Diedrich Knickerbocker (1809), promoted with a hoax about the missing historian.

"Rip Van Winkle" is in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. Irving wrote it overnight in Birmingham, England, staying with his sister Sarah and her husband Henry van Wart. He lived abroad for 17 years (1815-1832).

He served as U.S. Minister to Spain (1842-1846), lived at Sunnyside, and is buried in Sleepy Hollow cemetery (Dec 1, 1859). He encouraged writers such as Hawthorne, Melville, Longfellow and Poe, though Poe called him "much over-rated".

Legacy: called the first American man of letters and the first to earn a living by his pen; he advocated copyright protection, popularized "Gotham", is credited with the phrase "the almighty dollar", and helped shape the American image of St. Nicholas and Christmas. His Columbus biography also spread the flat-Earth myth.

concepts.intro: The last page of your Literary Terms packet gives a timeline and movement definitions. Historical-context questions can ask you to place a work in its period.
b: Puritanism 1620-1770s (plain style; obedience to God; journals, sermons, poems). Neoclassic 1770s to early 1800s (rationalism, the Age of Reason).
Romanticism early 1800s-1870s: a revolt against Rationalism. Realism 1850s-early 1900s. Regionalism 1884-early 1900s. Naturalism late 1800s-mid 1900s. Modernism 1920s-1945. Post-Modernism 1945 on.

Transcendentalism: a 19th-century movement in the Romantic tradition holding that every individual can reach ultimate truths through spiritual intuition, which transcends reason and sensory experience.
Rationalism: truth reached by reason instead of the authority of the past, the Church or an institution (also called Neoclassicism or the Age of Reason).

Plain style: writing that stresses simplicity and clarity, the main form of the Puritan writers. Regionalism / local color: emphasis on a specific setting's speech, customs and landscape, as in Twain's dialect.

Place the texts: Hawthorne's Puritan Salem is set in the 1600s but written in the 1830s Romantic period; Irving, Keats, Poe, Hawthorne and Emerson are Romantic-era writers; Twain (1880) bridges toward Realism and Regionalism.

concepts.intro: Characterization is how a writer reveals a character's personality.
b: Direct characterization: the narrator tells you the personality (e.g., a "patient boy" and "quiet girl").
Indirect characterization shows personality. Remember STEAL: Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks.
Speech: what a character says and how. Thoughts: private thoughts and feelings. Effect on others: how other characters react. Actions: what the character does. Looks: appearance and dress.
For every example, write the type, the quote with a citation, and an explanation of what it reveals about the character.
Round characters are complex; flat characters have one or two traits. Static characters do not change; dynamic characters change because of the story's events (Goodman Brown is dynamic).

Apply it: Rip's henpecked life and the children's joy when he approaches (effect on others); Baker's dialect (speech); Roderick's appearance (looks); Brown's decision to hurry to his "evil purpose" (actions and thoughts).

concepts.l: A. A. Rubin's Poe-style poems (Lesson #2 handout)
concepts.intro: Rubin, a former teacher turned professional poet, wrote these poems to imitate Edgar Allan Poe. The class question: how does Rubin use allusion in his works?
b: "Night Walkers" won first place in a Poe-style contest: a speaker whistling through a graveyard walks all night with a ghost until daybreak, when "all ghosts must go away".

"The Widow's Walk" (first published July 29, 2021 in Love Letters to Poe) uses the refrain "round and round she goes" and repeated end lines to create a haunting, hypnotic sound; children invent stories about the widow, and the dead husband follows her without knowing he is dead.

"The Widow's Walk (1849)" is set at Cold Spring Harbor: a widow paces the roof waiting for a husband whose ship sank; his ghost returns at night and leaves at dawn. The year 1849 is the year Poe died.

Recurring Poe-like elements: ghosts, graveyards, the pale moon, night's "dark inky gloom", refrain and repetition, and a supernatural companion. These echo Poe's Gothic style and mood, which is the class's allusion question.
Use for practice: identify allusion, refrain, imagery and mood in short poems, then connect them to Poe's Gothic style in "The Fall of the House of Usher".

traps: Mixing up anthropomorphism (animals or living things given human traits) with personification (nonliving objects given human traits). The bluejays are anthropomorphism; the House of Usher's "eyes" are personification.
Studying "The Custom House" or The Scarlet Letter for this exam. The only Hawthorne text on Unit 1 is "Young Goodman Brown".
Retelling the plot instead of analyzing how the author's language creates the effect. Always tie a specific word or device to a purpose.
Treating "Young Goodman Brown" as clearly a dream or clearly real; the story's power comes from the ambiguity.
Reading the pronoun or the speaker too quickly: check who is talking and who is being addressed (Roderick to the narrator; Rip to the villagers; Angela to Porphyro).
Using dictionary meanings instead of the meaning that fits the line. For vocabulary in context, test each choice back in the sentence.
Putting events in the wrong order. For chronology questions, run a quick timeline in your head for each story before choosing.
Choosing an interpretation that is true in general but not supported by the quote. Pick the answer the quote itself supports.
fms: Six texts: Rip Van Winkle (Irving), Eve of St. Agnes (Keats), Fall of the House of Usher (Poe), Baker's Bluejay Yarn (Twain), Young Goodman Brown (Hawthorne), Emerson handout.
Anthropomorphism = animals/living things with human traits; personification = objects.
Answer = claim + text evidence + how the words create the effect + purpose.
Question types: speaker/addressee, pronoun, word meaning, best interpretation, would agree/disagree, all-true-EXCEPT, chronology, accuracy, plot recall, historical context.
STEAL: Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks (indirect characterization).

flashcards.d: A framework for analyzing a text's rhetorical situation: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone.
The specific problem, need, or urgency that makes a piece of writing necessary at that moment.
What the writer wants the audience to think, feel, or do — always phrased as 'to ___.'
Limits on a writer, such as word count, audience expectations, or what's appropriate for the occasion.
An appeal to credibility and character — why the audience should trust the speaker.
An appeal to emotion, designed to make the audience feel something that moves them toward the writer's position.
An appeal to logic and reason, using facts, statistics, and clear chains of reasoning.
A logical fallacy that attacks the person making an argument instead of the argument itself.
A logical fallacy that misrepresents an opponent's argument as weaker than it really is, then attacks that weak version.
A logical fallacy presenting only two options when more actually exist.
Repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses or sentences.
Placing two contrasting ideas in a parallel grammatical structure.
Placing two things side by side to highlight their differences.
A direct comparison between two unlike things, without using 'like' or 'as.'
A question asked for effect rather than to get a literal answer, leading the reader to a conclusion.
A word's literal, dictionary definition.
The emotional association attached to a word, beyond its literal meaning.
How a writer arranges words and constructs sentences — a rhetorical choice in itself.
The writer's attitude toward the subject, revealed through diction and syntax; it can shift within a passage.
An argument that something is good, bad, right, or wrong.
Analysis that explains WHY evidence matters and HOW it supports the argument — different from summary.
The logical thread connecting a thesis through each piece of evidence to a coherent overall argument.
A specific, arguable claim that someone could reasonably disagree with — the core of an essay's argument.
Acknowledging a valid point on the opposing side of an argument before pivoting back to your own position.
Directly refuting an opposing point by explaining why it's flawed or less compelling.
An essay that develops the writer's own argument using at least three provided sources as support.
Organizing a synthesis essay by summarizing each source in turn instead of by the writer's own claims — a major weakness.
An essay explaining HOW a writer builds their argument and its effect on the audience, not whether the reader agrees.
The core rhetorical analysis skill: identify a specific choice, then explain its effect on the audience.
An essay defending the writer's own position on an issue using the writer's own knowledge, with no provided sources.
