Demonstrating nuance, qualification, or broader implications in an argument — beyond a simple thesis-evidence structure.
An error joining two independent clauses with only a comma; fix with a period, semicolon, or conjunction.
A group of words missing a subject, verb, or complete thought, unable to stand alone as a sentence.
Items in a list or series sharing the same grammatical form.
Independent clauses joined with no punctuation or connector at all.
Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone - a checklist for naming the rhetorical situation.
The urgent problem, event, or issue that prompts a writer to respond; the 'why now.'
The opportune moment: fitting the argument to the right time, audience, and circumstances.
The relationship among speaker (ethos), audience (pathos), and subject/message (logos).
The beliefs, conventions, prior events, and limits that shape and restrict a writer's possible response.
Always a verb phrase: 'to convince [specific audience] that/to ___.'
Identifying the specific readers' values, assumptions, and knowledge so appeals can be aimed at them.
Appeals to the speaker's credibility, the audience's emotions, and logical reasoning, respectively.
Attacking the person making an argument instead of the argument itself.
Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack.
Presenting only two options when more exist.
Assuming that because one event followed another, the first caused the second.
Drawing a broad conclusion from too little or unrepresentative evidence.
Citing an authority as support; a fallacy when the authority is irrelevant or offered as the sole proof.
Deductive: general principle to specific conclusion. Inductive: specific cases to a general (provisional) claim.
The character a writer projects through language, tone, and stance - not the same as the real author.
Repetition of a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses, building momentum.
Repetition of a word or phrase at the end of successive clauses.
Contrasting ideas placed in parallel grammatical structure.
A reversal of grammatical structure in successive phrases ('ask not what... what you can do...').
Omitting conjunctions between items in a list, speeding the pace ('I came, I saw, I conquered').
Repeating conjunctions between items ('and... and... and'), slowing the pace and adding weight.
A metaphor states a comparison directly; a simile uses 'like' or 'as.'
A single comparison developed across multiple sentences or an entire passage.
A brief reference to a known text, person, or event that imports its authority or emotion.
Understatement by negating the opposite ('not a small problem'), often for dry emphasis.
Saying the opposite of what is meant, expecting the audience to catch the gap; sarcasm is a pointed form.
A writer's word choice, including the connotations those words carry.
Denotation is the literal meaning; connotation is the emotional or cultural association.
The arrangement of words into sentences: length, order, and structure.
The writer's attitude toward the subject or audience; name it precisely (wry, indignant, elegiac).
A change in attitude within a text, often marked by 'but,' a paragraph break, or a change in sentence length; it signals a turn in the argument.
Withholds the main clause until the end, building suspense and emphasis.
States the main clause first, then adds modifying phrases and detail.
What a writer chooses to include or omit; itself a form of argument.
Language that appeals to the senses, making an abstraction vivid and felt.
Fact (is it true?), value (is it good?), and policy (what should we do?).
Summary restates what the evidence says; commentary explains HOW it supports the claim.
The logical progression connecting thesis, sub-claims, and evidence.
Narrowing a claim with words like 'often,' 'in most cases,' or a condition, so it fits the evidence.
Relevant evidence bears on the exact claim; sufficient evidence is enough, and varied enough, to be credible.
Acknowledging that an opposing point has some merit without abandoning the thesis.
Specific and arguable; it previews a line of reasoning rather than stating an obvious truth.
Begin a sentence with familiar information and end with the new point, to create flow.
Grant an opposing point, then explain why it does not defeat the thesis ('While X is true, it does not follow that Y').
Words that must name the logical relationship between ideas (however, therefore, for instance), not just decorate.
Chronological, cause-effect, problem-solution, comparison-contrast, and climactic (order of importance).
The quality of prose that guides the reader from idea to idea without gaps; aided by repeated key terms and clear referents.
Build an argument using at least three of the provided sources as evidence, cited clearly.
Walking through sources one by one instead of organizing body paragraphs around your own claims.
A signal phrase names the source in the sentence ('Source B argues'); a parenthetical puts it at the end ((Source B)).
A clear, arguable, often qualified position that the sources can be used to support.
Use one source to complicate or answer another within a paragraph built on your claim.
Explain HOW a writer argues and to what effect - not whether you agree with the argument.
Weak: lists devices ('uses ethos, pathos, logos'). Strong: names what the writer does and to what end.
Naming a strategy and quoting a line without explaining its effect on the audience and purpose.
On a timed essay, analyze 2-3 strategies thoroughly rather than listing many.
The core structure of a body paragraph: identify a choice, quote the text, explain the effect.
Take and defend your own position using your own reasoning and evidence (no provided sources).
Refutation directly answers an opposing argument and shows why it fails; concession grants it partial merit.
Nuance, attention to complexity or context, and answering 'so what?' - rewarded on the AP rubric.
One or two well-developed, analyzed examples usually score higher than many shallow ones.
Two independent clauses joined by only a comma; fix with a period, semicolon, or conjunction.
Items in a series or comparison must match in grammatical form.
A colon follows a complete clause and introduces an explanation or list; a semicolon joins two independent clauses.
Usually reward the clearest and most concise option, not the longest or most formal.
'past history,' 'end result,' 'the reason ... is because,' 'in order to' when 'to' works.
Verify every answer choice against the exact wording and context of the passage.
Tuesday 10/6. Great American Short Stories, Literary Devices packet, nonfiction and handouts; only Hawthorne text is "Young Goodman Brown".
A movement reacting against Enlightenment rationalism that values emotion, imagination, nature, the individual, the past and the supernatural.
The order-and-reason outlook (rationalism, restraint, science) that Romanticism pushed against.
American Romantic author (1783-1859) of "Rip Van Winkle", first published in The Sketch Book under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon.
The fictional historian whose papers frame "Rip Van Winkle" (Irving's playful fake-history device).

flashcards.t: Rip Van Winkle: setting and time frame
flashcards.d: A Dutch village in the Catskills; Rip sleeps 20 years from British rule under George III into the new American republic.
Rip's wife, characterized as a shrewish "termagant"/"virago"; Irving's language invites sympathy for Rip.
Rip's dog and loyal companion, part of the sympathetic characterization of Rip as easygoing.

flashcards.t: What Irving comments on through Rip's sleep
flashcards.d: The changes from colony to independent nation: new flag, political arguing, and a village that no longer recognizes him.

flashcards.t: The Eve of St. Agnes: legend
flashcards.d: On St. Agnes' Eve (Jan 20), a young woman who follows the rituals may dream of her future husband.

flashcards.t: The Eve of St. Agnes: main characters
flashcards.d: Madeline (the dreamer), Porphyro (her lover from a hostile family), Angela (the old nurse), the Beadsman (opens and closes the poem).
Nine-line stanza rhymed ABABBCBCC, eight lines of iambic pentameter then a longer last line; used throughout Keats's poem.
English Romantic poet (1795-1821); wrote "The Eve of St. Agnes" in 1819 (published 1820).
American Gothic and Romantic writer (1809-1849); "The Fall of the House of Usher" (1839).
The ill, hypersensitive host whose nerves and mind mirror the decaying house.
Roderick's twin sister; entombed while appearing dead; her return precedes the collapse.
Both the physical mansion and the family line; the fissure and collapse show the family's end.
Poem inside Usher: a once-fair palace of Thought overrun by "evil things"; it mirrors Roderick's mind.
The romance the narrator reads to Roderick; sounds in it echo real noises, foreshadowing Madeline's return.
Poe's idea that every detail in a story should build one single emotional impact (in Usher, dread).
Genre with gloomy settings, decay, madness, death and the supernatural; strong mood.
Samuel Clemens (1835-1910); wrote "Baker's Bluejay Yarn" (1880), a humorous tall tale.
A tale, especially a long story of adventure or incredible happenings, often exaggerated.
A middle-aged, simple-hearted California miner who tells Twain that bluejays are the most human and best-talking animals.
Giving animate (living) beings human characteristics, like Baker's talking, swearing bluejays.
Giving inanimate (nonliving) objects human characteristics, like the house's "eye-like windows".
Putting two things side by side for effect, such as Baker's earnest tone against a ridiculous tale.

Baker's centerpiece: a jay drops acorns into a hole in a cabin roof that leads into an empty house; five thousand jays laugh when they see the acorns on the floor. Possible metaphor for foolish human effort.
Writing that captures a region or group's speech; builds Baker's characterization and humor.
American Dark Romantic (1804-1864); "Young Goodman Brown" (1835) is his only work on Unit 1.
Puritan Salem Village, Massachusetts; the story moves from town to the dark forest and back.
Brown's wife and the loss of his religious faith; the pink ribbons are her symbol of innocence.
A staff shaped like a black serpent; a Biblical allusion to the serpent in Eden, marking the traveler as the devil.
Hawthorne never confirms whether the forest meeting was a dream or real, leaving the theme of doubt and hypocrisy open.
A brief, indirect reference to a person, place, text or idea of historical, cultural, literary or political significance; relies on the reader's knowledge.
Hints or clues about events that come later.
An object, person or action that stands for a larger idea, like Faith's pink ribbons.
A story in which characters, settings and events stand for moral, spiritual or political ideas.
Direct: the narrator states traits. Indirect: traits shown through actions, speech, thoughts, appearance and others' reactions.
Who tells the story (first person, third limited, omniscient); shapes what we know and trust.
Mood: the feeling created in the reader. Tone: the author's attitude toward the subject.
Leading Transcendentalist (1803-1882); the handout is from "The Transcendentalist".

Emerson excerpt: the materialist starts from the external world and respects society and social institutions; the idealist (transcendentalist) starts from consciousness and holds that "Mind is the only reality".

flashcards.t: James Truslow Adams and the American Dream
flashcards.d: Popularized the phrase in The Epic of America (1931): opportunity for each person according to ability, a fuller life for everyone, more than material wealth.
An open-ended, text-based question that prompts discussion, not a recall question. Start: To what extent, In what ways, For what reasons, How is/does and why is it significant?
Underline evidence, circle the key word, label the mood, and annotate how the words work together.
A violent, overbearing, quarrelsome woman; Irving's word for Dame Van Winkle.
A domineering, ill-tempered woman; another word Irving uses for Dame.
An impossible-to-overcome strong dislike; Rip's attitude toward profitable labor.
Obsequious: fawning, overly eager to please. Conciliating: trying to win over or calm.
Brisk, cheerful readiness or eagerness.
Ruddy; having a healthy reddish color.
A small group or faction, often political, that joins together in secret or for a shared aim.
Approval or praise.
With hands on hips and elbows turned out.
Inherited from one's father or ancestors.
Relating to marriage.
Noisy, boisterous revelers.
A man paid or bound to pray for others' souls; the cold, praying old man in Keats's poem.
Seraph: an angelic being of the highest order. Pinion: a wing or flight feather. Ramparts: protective earthen or stone walls of a fortress.
Discordant: harsh, disagreeing, out of tune. Throng: a large crowd.
Five methods of indirect characterization: Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks.
Static: does not change much in the story. Dynamic: changes in an important way because of the story's action.
Flat: one or two traits, one-dimensional. Round: complex, with many dimensions like real people.
Puritanism (1620-1770s), Neoclassic (1770s-early 1800s), Romanticism (early 1800s-1870s), Realism (1850s-early 1900s).
A 19th-century movement in the Romantic tradition holding that every individual can reach ultimate truths through spiritual intuition, which transcends reason and sensory experience.
Credited with founding Gothic fiction with The Castle of Otranto (1764), subtitled "A Gothic Story".
Wordsworth and Coleridge's 1790s collection that began English Romanticism; Wordsworth's Preface called poetry "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings".
Irving's first pen name (1802 letters) and the 1807 magazine that nicknamed New York "Gotham".
The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. (1819-20), the collection containing "Rip Van Winkle" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow".
Irving's home on the Hudson where he lived after returning from Spain; he is buried at Sleepy Hollow cemetery nearby.
The explorer whose crew, per the villagers, still haunt the Catskills and bowl ninepins, explaining the thunder.
Rip's grown daughter; Rip tells her he is her father, and she takes him in to live with her family.
The most ancient inhabitant, descended from a historian of the province, who recognizes Rip and corroborates the legend of Hendrick Hudson's crew.

flashcards.t: Union Hotel and the sign of General Washington
flashcards.d: The changed inn and sign in Rip's village show the switch from King George III to the new republic.
The question Rip is asked on his return; he does not understand the new political parties and answers as a loyal subject of the King.
The jay's exaggerated claim of how many acorns he dropped in the hole; hyperbole that fuels the yarn's humor.
The hole led into a cabin; the door is open and acorns are scattered on the floor, revealing the jay's absurd task.
The 1675-76 New England conflict alluded to when the traveler says Brown's father burned an Indian village.
The Puritan-era events behind Hawthorne's Salem setting; his ancestor John Hathorne was a judge.
Simple, clear writing stressing obedience to God; the main form of Puritan writers per the packet.
A word, phrase or line repeated for effect, like "round and round she goes" in Rubin's "The Widow's Walk".
An outrageously exaggerated, humorous story that is obviously unbelievable, like Baker's yarn.
Verbal: says one thing, means another. Situational: outcome differs from what is expected. Dramatic: the reader knows more than the character.
Deliberately suggesting two or more different, sometimes conflicting, meanings; on purpose it is a device, not vagueness.
Poe's story in the Philadelphia Saturday Courier (Jan 14, 1832) where he first used the single-effect technique on which the modern short story is built.
The technique of building every detail toward one preconceived impression, with the action focused on the climactic moment and the mood controlled from first to last.
Henry Seidel Canby's phrase for the moral or intellectual weight Hawthorne added to the American short story.
Poe's detective-style tale of reasoning, the parent of the detective story ("The Murders in the Rue Morgue").
Irving: an orderly tale of linked incidents in chronological order, graceful, humorous, urbane. Poe: a concentrated tale of a single, preconceived effect.
The Introduction says Usher and "Young Goodman Brown" both move from light into darkness and back into light; Poe's darkness is theatrical, Hawthorne's is the darkness of the soul.
Henry James's phrase for the probing story that Hawthorne began: less a complication resolved than an exposed situation.
The Introduction says Twain mastered the humorous frontier sketch and the fable; "Bluejay Yarn" is superb in its own kind and links to Uncle Remus and Thurber.
Writing that emphasizes a specific place's speech, customs and landscape; the Introduction credits Bret Harte's "The Luck of Roaring Camp" (1868) with popularizing the short story.
Pestilent: harmful, troublesome. Patrimonial: inherited from a father. Urchin: a mischievous small child (all describing Rip's farm and son).
Steady, careful diligence (Rip has plenty of it, but only for idle pursuits like fishing).
Confusing, hard-to-understand language; Rip cannot follow the election talk.
A state of inactivity or deep sleep; Irving's word for Rip's twenty-year sleep.
To confirm; Peter Vanderdonk corroborates Rip's story.
I pray thee; afraid; stay or wait (from Faith's plea in "Young Goodman Brown").
Scruples: moral doubts. Anathema: a formal curse or denunciation.
Benighted: in darkness, physical or moral. Wanton: immoral, reckless, unrestrained.
Wordiness; a crack; a small mountain lake; corpse-like paleness (Poe's Usher vocabulary).
Twain's term for stupid or thick-headed, describing the jays' opinions about the hole.
The silent landlord whose opinions control the idle bench-sitters at the inn; he has died eighteen years before Rip's return.
Per Peter Vanderdonk, the explorer and his crew keep a vigil in the Kaatskills every twenty years; the thunder is their ninepins.
Henpecked husbands wish for "a quieting draught out of Rip Van Winkle's flagon" (p. 51).
Respected Salem figures Brown sees in the forest; Cloyse taught him his catechism.
A woman at the forest ceremony who "received the devil's promise to be queen of hell"; her name is that of an actual Salem witch-trial defendant.
Brown's cry when the pink ribbon falls; followed by "There is no good on earth; and sin is but a name. Come, devil!"

flashcards.t: Quotation: "We have put her living in the tomb!"
flashcards.d: Roderick's confession to the narrator that he heard Madeline moving in the coffin (p. 90).
The jay's first delighted reaction to the knot-hole in the cabin roof (Baker's yarn).
The jay's boast of how many acorns he dropped; hyperbole in Baker's yarn.

quiz.q: In SOAPSTone, what does the 'P' stand for?
quiz.e: P stands for Purpose — what the writer wants the audience to think, feel, or do.

quiz.q: A politician gives a eulogy at a colleague's funeral. What is the OCCASION?
o: The colleague's death and the funeral service
quiz.e: Occasion is the event that prompts the writing — here, the death and funeral.

quiz.q: Which best states a text's PURPOSE?
o: To persuade parents to limit screen time
quiz.e: Purpose must be phrased as an infinitive verb phrase describing the intended effect on the audience.

quiz.q: What is exigence?
o: The urgent problem or need that makes a piece of writing necessary
quiz.e: Exigence is the specific urgency or problem prompting the writing.

quiz.q: A textbook chapter and a passionate op-ed can share the same subject but differ in what?
quiz.e: Two texts can share a subject but differ completely in purpose and tone.

quiz.q: Which is a CONSTRAINT on a writer?
o: A strict word limit for a newspaper column
quiz.e: Constraints are limits like word count, format, or audience expectations.

quiz.q: 'Skeptical, yet hopeful' is an example of what SOAPSTone element?
quiz.e: This describes the writer's attitude — tone.

quiz.q: Identifying a speech's specific intended audience (rather than 'everyone') is important because:
o: Rhetorical choices are tailored to a specific audience's values and knowledge
quiz.e: Writers tailor their rhetorical choices to a specific audience, not a generic one.

quiz.q: A company's product recall letter is an example of what shaping the occasion?
o: A specific real-world event requiring a response
quiz.e: The recall itself is the event/occasion prompting the letter.

quiz.q: Which correctly separates SUBJECT from PURPOSE?
o: Subject: climate change. Purpose: to mobilize young voters.
Subject: to persuade. Purpose: climate change.
Subject and purpose are always identical.
Subject is the audience; purpose is the tone.
quiz.e: Subject is the topic; purpose is the intended effect — they must be stated separately.

quiz.q: A CEO's shareholder letter written just after a scandal is shaped mostly by what exigence?
o: The need to respond to and address the scandal
quiz.e: The scandal creates the urgent need (exigence) prompting this specific letter.

quiz.q: Which SOAPSTone element asks 'who is writing or speaking?'
quiz.e: Speaker identifies who is behind the text and what we know about them.

quiz.q: A formal court filing versus a casual text message about the same event differ mainly in what?
o: Register and constraints appropriate to the occasion
quiz.e: The occasion and its constraints shape register/formality even when the underlying subject is the same.

quiz.q: Why is 'the audience is everyone' usually a weak rhetorical analysis claim?
o: Effective rhetoric is normally shaped for a specific, identifiable audience
All texts are legally required to target one group
quiz.e: Strong analysis identifies a specific intended audience the rhetorical choices are shaped for.

quiz.q: Which is the best description of TONE, not just a single word?
o: Wry and gently mocking, shifting to sincere in the final paragraph
quiz.e: Tone should be described precisely, and can shift across a passage.

quiz.q: A letter to the editor responding to a specific recent news event best illustrates:
o: Exigence driving the occasion for writing
quiz.e: The recent news event is the exigence prompting the letter.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes SPEAKER from the actual author in some rhetorical texts (e.g., a persona)?
o: The speaker is the voice/persona presented in the text, which may differ from the biographical author
Speaker refers only to spoken speeches
quiz.e: In some texts a constructed persona speaks, distinct from the historical author.

quiz.q: Which SOAPSTone element would you use to analyze WHY a writer chose formal academic language?
quiz.e: Register often reflects choices shaped by both intended audience and occasion.

quiz.q: A graduation speech given right after a school tragedy would have its content most shaped by:
o: The specific exigence of the tragedy
quiz.e: The tragedy is the driving exigence shaping the speech's content and tone.

quiz.q: Which correctly identifies constraints in an opinion column limited to 800 words for a general newspaper audience?
o: Word count and audience expectations for the publication
quiz.e: Word limits and audience/publication norms are classic constraints.

quiz.q: An appeal based on the speaker's credentials and trustworthiness is:
quiz.e: Ethos is the appeal to the speaker's credibility and character.

quiz.q: A charity ad showing images of hungry children to evoke sympathy relies primarily on:
quiz.e: Vivid, emotional imagery designed to evoke sympathy is a pathos appeal.

quiz.q: A doctor citing peer-reviewed studies to support a health claim uses primarily:
o: Logos, supported by ethos from expertise
quiz.e: Data/studies are logos; the doctor's expertise also lends ethos.

quiz.q: 'If we allow students one retake, soon no test will ever count' is an example of:
quiz.e: This claims an extreme, unjustified chain reaction from one small step — a slippery slope.

quiz.q: 'My opponent wants to cut this program, so he clearly hates poor families' misrepresents the opponent's actual position. This is:
quiz.e: This exaggerates/distorts the opponent's real position to attack a weaker version — a straw man.

quiz.q: 'Either we ban the product entirely, or we do nothing at all' ignores middle-ground options. This is:
quiz.e: Presenting only two extreme options when others exist is a false dilemma.

quiz.q: Attacking a scientist's argument by mocking their appearance instead of their data is:
quiz.e: Attacking the person rather than the argument is ad hominem.

quiz.q: 'I met three rude tourists from that city, so everyone from there must be rude' is a:
quiz.e: Drawing a broad conclusion from too small a sample is a hasty generalization.

quiz.q: A speaker who fairly acknowledges the opposing view before responding builds:
o: Ethos, by appearing reasonable and fair
quiz.e: Fair acknowledgment of opposing views builds credibility/ethos.

quiz.q: Which is the best full analysis, not just labeling?
o: The statistic builds logos, making the argument feel objective and hard to dispute
quiz.e: Strong analysis explains the effect of the device, not just names it.

quiz.q: A veteran discussing the human cost of war through a personal story primarily appeals to:
o: Pathos, and secondarily ethos from firsthand experience
quiz.e: Personal storytelling evokes emotion (pathos) while firsthand experience also builds ethos.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of Aristotle's three appeals?
quiz.e: The three classical appeals are ethos, pathos, and logos; kairos (timing) is a related but separate rhetorical concept.

quiz.q: Using vivid, charged language ('this catastrophe will devastate families') primarily builds:
quiz.e: Emotionally charged language is designed to evoke feeling — pathos.

quiz.q: 'You can't trust her tax plan, she's not even an economist' dismisses her plan based only on her credentials rather than its content. This mixes:
o: Ad hominem-style dismissal disguised as an ethos critique
quiz.e: Dismissing an argument based only on the person's background, without engaging the actual plan, echoes ad hominem reasoning.

quiz.q: A well-supported ethos appeal is generally built through:
o: Demonstrated expertise, fairness, and careful language
quiz.e: Ethos is built through expertise, fairness, and precise, careful language.

quiz.q: Which best explains why using pathos is NOT automatically a logical fallacy?
o: Emotional appeals can be a legitimate, valid rhetorical strategy alongside logic
All emotional appeals are inherently dishonest
quiz.e: Pathos is a legitimate classical appeal; it becomes a fallacy only when it replaces valid reasoning deceptively.

quiz.q: 'Studies from three major universities all found the same result' primarily supports:
quiz.e: Multiple corroborating studies is evidence-based reasoning — logos.

quiz.q: Identify the fallacy: 'We must ban video games entirely, or violence will completely destroy society.'
o: False dilemma combined with slippery slope
quiz.e: This presents only two extremes (false dilemma) and an unjustified extreme chain (slippery slope).

quiz.q: On the exam, why is simply writing 'this is pathos' insufficient?
o: It doesn't explain HOW the appeal functions or its effect on the audience
Ethos is the only appeal that matters
quiz.e: Analysis must connect the device to its specific effect, not just name it.

quiz.q: 'I have a dream... I have a dream... I have a dream' at the start of successive sentences is:
quiz.e: Repetition at the BEGINNING of successive clauses is anaphora.

quiz.q: '...government of the people, by the people, for the people' repeats a phrase at the END of clauses. This is:
quiz.e: Repetition at the END of successive clauses/phrases is epistrophe.

quiz.q: 'Ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country' reverses grammatical structure. This is:
quiz.e: A reversal of grammatical structure across clauses is chiasmus.

quiz.q: 'The classroom was a zoo' is an example of:
quiz.e: A direct comparison without 'like' or 'as' is a metaphor.

quiz.q: 'The wind whispered through the trees' gives human qualities to wind. This is:
quiz.e: Giving human qualities to something nonhuman is personification.

quiz.q: 'Brave as a lion' uses which figure of speech?
quiz.e: A comparison using 'as' (or 'like') is a simile.

quiz.q: 'I've told you a million times' is:
quiz.e: Deliberate exaggeration for effect is hyperbole.

quiz.q: Calling a disastrous storm 'a bit of bad weather' is an example of:
quiz.e: Deliberately downplaying something for effect is understatement.

quiz.q: 'Do you really think that plan will work?' asked with no expectation of a literal answer is a:
quiz.e: A question asked for effect, not a literal answer, is rhetorical.

quiz.q: Saying 'Great job' sarcastically after someone makes a mistake is an example of:
quiz.e: Saying the opposite of what is meant, often to criticize, is verbal irony.

quiz.q: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' places two contrasting ideas in parallel structure. This is:
quiz.e: Placing contrasting ideas in parallel grammatical structure is antithesis.

quiz.q: Placing a description of extreme wealth directly next to a description of extreme poverty to highlight the contrast is:
quiz.e: Placing two things side by side to highlight contrast is juxtaposition.

quiz.q: 'She has a heart of stone' is:
quiz.e: A direct comparison ('heart' equated with 'stone') without 'like/as' is a metaphor.

quiz.q: Repeating the last word of one clause at the start of the next ('Fear leads to anger. Anger leads to hate.') is:
quiz.e: Repeating the final word of one clause at the start of the next is anadiplosis.

quiz.q: Naming 'anaphora' correctly but never explaining its effect earns:
o: Little credit — effect must always be explained
No credit is ever given for identifying devices
quiz.e: Identification alone is insufficient; effect on the reader/argument must be explained.

quiz.q: Which requires attention to CONTEXT to correctly identify?
quiz.e: Irony depends on context contradicting the literal words, unlike devices identifiable from wording alone.

quiz.q: 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' from Macbeth is an example of:
quiz.e: This places contrasting ideas ('fair'/'foul') in a balanced, reversed structure.

quiz.q: A list of parallel infinitive phrases ('to run, to jump, to swim') used for rhythm and balance is:
quiz.e: Repeating a grammatical structure across a series is parallelism.

quiz.q: Which distinguishes simile from metaphor?
o: Simile uses 'like' or 'as'; metaphor makes a direct comparison without them
quiz.e: The comparison word 'like'/'as' is present in a simile but absent in a metaphor.

quiz.q: 'The stars danced in the night sky' is:
quiz.e: Giving stars the human action of dancing is personification.

quiz.q: 'Slender' and 'skinny' can share a denotation but differ in:
o: Tone only, unrelated to word choice
quiz.e: They describe the same literal quality but carry different emotional associations — connotation.

quiz.q: A word's literal, dictionary meaning is its:
quiz.e: Denotation is a word's literal definition.

quiz.q: Choosing elevated, precise vocabulary over casual everyday words reflects:
quiz.e: Elevated, precise word choice is formal diction.

quiz.q: A string of short, blunt sentences in a row typically creates:
quiz.e: Short sentences often create emphasis, bluntness, or urgency.

quiz.q: A single long sentence with many clauses piling on top of each other can create a sense of:
quiz.e: Long, complex sentences can build accumulation or momentum.

quiz.q: A deliberate sentence fragment used for effect creates:
o: Dramatic emphasis on a single idea
A shift to a new subject
quiz.e: Fragments used deliberately draw sharp emphasis to an isolated idea.

quiz.q: Mixing short and long sentences throughout a passage primarily controls:
quiz.e: Sentence variety controls pacing and keeps the reader engaged.

quiz.q: A transition word like 'however' appearing mid-passage most likely signals:
quiz.e: Contrast transitions often mark a shift in tone or idea.

quiz.q: Which is the more precise tone word?
quiz.e: PrecisStudye tone words like 'indignant' are stronger than vague words like 'bad' or 'negative.'

quiz.q: Writing in first person ('I believe...') primarily creates:
quiz.e: First person creates a personal, intimate connection and speaker authority.

quiz.q: Writing in third person, avoiding 'I,' typically creates a sense of:
quiz.e: Third person tends to create distance and an impression of objectivity.

quiz.q: The combination of a writer's characteristic diction, syntax, and tone is called their:
quiz.e: Style is the recognizable combination of diction, syntax, and tone across a writer's work.

quiz.q: Concrete, sensory diction ('the acrid smell of smoke') mainly creates:
quiz.e: Concrete, sensory words create vivid images for the reader.

quiz.q: Abstract diction ('justice,' 'freedom,' 'progress') tends to create a more:
quiz.e: Abstract, conceptual words create a more analytical, less sensory tone.

quiz.q: How formal or informal language is, relative to the occasion, is called:
quiz.e: Register describes the formality level of language relative to context.

quiz.q: A passage that starts admiring and shifts to critical midway shows:
quiz.e: This is a clear example of a tone shift within a single passage.

quiz.q: Which is a mistake to avoid when discussing syntax and diction?
o: Discussing them as separate observations unconnected to tone
quiz.e: Diction and syntax should be discussed as tools that build tone, not in isolation.

quiz.q: Assuming short sentences always signal 'simple ideas' is a mistake because:
o: Short sentences are often used to emphasize complex or weighty ideas
Short sentences are never used for emphasis
quiz.e: Short sentences frequently emphasize complex or weighty points, not just simple ones.

quiz.q: 'The committee shall convene' vs. 'let's get together' differ mainly in:
quiz.e: These phrases describe the same action with very different formal vs. casual diction/register.

quiz.q: An argument claiming something is TRUE or FALSE and can be verified is a claim of:
quiz.e: A claim of fact asserts something verifiable as true or false.

quiz.q: 'The school should ban cell phones during class' is a claim of:
quiz.e: Arguing something SHOULD or should NOT be done is a claim of policy.

quiz.q: 'Cheating is morally wrong' is a claim of:
quiz.e: Arguing something is good, bad, right, or wrong is a claim of value.

quiz.q: A specific personal story used to make an abstract point concrete is:
quiz.e: A specific story/example is anecdotal evidence.

quiz.q: Citing a peer-reviewed study's data supports an argument primarily through:
quiz.e: Numerical/data-based evidence is statistical evidence.

quiz.q: Quoting a leading scientist's opinion on climate change borrows credibility through:
quiz.e: Citing an authority's opinion is expert testimony, which lends ethos.

quiz.q: Restating what evidence says without explaining its significance is:
quiz.e: Restating WHAT evidence says, without explanation, is summary.

quiz.q: Explaining WHY a piece of evidence supports the thesis is:
quiz.e: Analysis explaining why evidence matters is commentary.

quiz.q: A recommended ratio of evidence to commentary in a strong paragraph is roughly:
o: One sentence of evidence to two or more of commentary
Five sentences of evidence to one of commentary
quiz.e: Strong paragraphs favor more commentary/analysis than raw evidence.

quiz.q: The logical thread connecting a thesis through evidence to a coherent argument is called the:
quiz.e: This is the definition of a line of reasoning.

quiz.q: Each body paragraph in a strong essay should:
o: Advance a different part of the argument
Repeat the same point with new evidence
quiz.e: Paragraphs should build the argument forward, not repeat the same point.

quiz.q: Evidence presented without ever connecting back to the thesis is a weakness because:
o: The reader shouldn't have to guess why the evidence was included
quiz.e: Every piece of evidence needs explicit commentary connecting it to the thesis.

quiz.q: A strong thesis usually combines which claim types?
o: Elements of fact, value, and/or policy as needed for a specific position
quiz.e: Strong theses often blend claim types into one specific, arguable position.

quiz.q: Which is the best example of commentary, not summary?
o: This statistic reveals how widespread the problem truly is, undermining the claim that it's rare
quiz.e: This explains the significance of the evidence rather than just restating it.

quiz.q: A paragraph that only restates evidence in different words, without analysis, is best described as:
quiz.e: Restating evidence without analysis is summary, not commentary.

quiz.q: Why is repeating the same underlying point across multiple paragraphs a weakness?
o: It fails to build a genuine line of reasoning that advances the argument
It strengthens the thesis through repetition
It is required by AP graders
quiz.e: Genuine line of reasoning requires each paragraph to add something new.

quiz.q: Which type of evidence draws a parallel to a past event to support a claim?
quiz.e: Referencing a past event or precedent is historical evidence.

quiz.q: 'So what?' is the question that commentary should answer because it:
o: Explains why the evidence proves the claim and matters to the reader
Should never be asked in an essay
quiz.e: Commentary should always explain the significance ('so what') of the evidence.

quiz.q: A claim asserting 'social media usage has tripled since 2015' is a claim of:
quiz.e: This is a verifiable factual claim.

quiz.q: Which best shows a logical LINE OF REASONING across paragraphs?
o: Paragraph 1 establishes the problem's scope; paragraph 2 explains its cause; paragraph 3 proposes a solution
All three paragraphs repeat the same statistic
Only the introduction contains a claim
quiz.e: Each paragraph builds a distinct, connected part of the overall argument.

quiz.q: An effective thesis should be:
quiz.e: An effective thesis takes a specific, defensible position someone could disagree with.

quiz.q: 'In this essay, I will discuss climate change' is a weak thesis because it:
o: Announces intent instead of taking an arguable position
quiz.e: This merely announces the topic rather than making a claim.

quiz.q: A topic sentence should:
o: State the paragraph's specific claim, not just announce a topic
quiz.e: A strong topic sentence makes a specific claim, guiding the paragraph's argument.

quiz.q: Acknowledging a valid point on the opposing side before returning to your own argument is called:
quiz.e: Acknowledging a fair opposing point is a concession.

quiz.q: Directly refuting an opposing point by explaining its flaw is called:
quiz.e: Explaining why an opposing point is flawed or less compelling is a rebuttal.

quiz.q: Ignoring the strongest counterarguments to your position tends to:
o: Weaken ethos by seeming one-sided or naive
quiz.e: Ignoring strong counterarguments makes the writer appear one-sided, weakening credibility.

quiz.q: A transition word should primarily show:
quiz.e: Transitions should reveal logical relationships like contrast or cause-effect, not just connect sentences.

quiz.q: 'Also' and 'another thing' are often weak transitions because they show:
o: Addition, but not the actual logical relationship between ideas
quiz.e: These words only signal addition, not deeper logical connections.

quiz.q: An effective conclusion typically:
o: Broadens the argument's significance beyond just restating the thesis
Simply repeats the introduction word for word
quiz.e: A strong conclusion extends significance rather than just repeating the thesis.

quiz.q: Introducing a completely new, unsupported argument in the conclusion is considered:
quiz.e: New unsupported arguments in a conclusion weaken structural coherence.

quiz.q: A body paragraph missing commentary that ties evidence back to the thesis is:
quiz.e: Every body paragraph needs commentary linking evidence explicitly to the thesis.

quiz.q: Why should an introduction establish context briefly before the thesis?
o: It orients the reader without delaying the argument unnecessarily
Thesis statements should come first, always
quiz.e: Brief context orients the reader efficiently before the thesis arrives.

quiz.q: A concession followed immediately by a strong rebuttal demonstrates:
o: Balanced, credible engagement with the opposing view
quiz.e: Concession + rebuttal shows fair, credible engagement with opposing views.

quiz.q: Which shows a genuine LOGICAL transition, not just addition?
quiz.e: 'Despite this' signals a clear logical (concessive/contrastive) relationship.

quiz.q: A thesis that simply restates a factual prompt statement is weak because it:
o: Isn't arguable — no one could reasonably disagree with a plain fact
quiz.e: A thesis must be arguable; a bare fact restatement isn't.

quiz.q: Which paragraph structure element ties the evidence back to the paragraph's claim?
quiz.e: Closing commentary should tie the evidence explicitly back to the thesis/claim.

quiz.q: A well-organized essay's paragraphs should:
o: Build on each other in a deliberate order
quiz.e: Deliberate paragraph order helps build a coherent, logical argument.

quiz.q: Which best represents a genuine counterargument being engaged, not dismissed?
o: Explaining the opposing view's strongest form, then explaining specifically why it falls short
Mentioning the opposing view in one dismissive clause
Restating your own thesis instead of the counterargument
quiz.e: Genuine engagement requires presenting the opposing view fairly before rebutting it.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes a concession from a rebuttal?
o: A concession acknowledges a valid opposing point; a rebuttal explains why a point is flawed
A rebuttal always comes before a concession
Concessions are never followed by rebuttals
quiz.e: Concession = acknowledge; rebuttal = refute — they are distinct, often paired, moves.

quiz.q: A conclusion that only repeats the thesis word-for-word is considered:
o: A missed opportunity to extend the argument's significance
quiz.e: Strong conclusions go beyond simple restatement to broaden significance.

quiz.q: The synthesis essay primarily requires the writer to:
o: Develop their own argument, supported by at least three provided sources
quiz.e: The synthesis essay is the writer's own argument, using sources as support.

quiz.q: What is the minimum number of sources that must be cited in the synthesis essay?
quiz.e: At least three of the provided sources must be cited.

quiz.q: Organizing a synthesis essay strictly source-by-source ('Source A says... Source B says...') is:
o: A common weakness — it becomes a summary rather than an argument
quiz.e: Source-by-source organization tends to become summary instead of a genuine argument.

quiz.q: A synthesis essay should be organized primarily around:
o: The writer's own claims, with sources woven in as support
Each source in the order given
quiz.e: Strong synthesis essays organize by the writer's own points, not by source.

quiz.q: Using a source to acknowledge and then rebut a counterargument is:
o: A valid strategic use of a source
Only for the rhetorical analysis essay
quiz.e: Sources can be used strategically to address counterarguments, not just support the main claim.

quiz.q: A 'qualified' thesis on the synthesis prompt (agreeing with conditions/nuance) is:
o: Completely acceptable and often stronger than an all-or-nothing stance
quiz.e: A specific, qualified position is a legitimate and often strong approach.

quiz.q: A vague thesis that doesn't commit to any real position on the synthesis prompt is:
o: A weakness — it isn't defensible or specific
quiz.e: Vague, noncommittal theses fail to take a defensible position.

quiz.q: Citing a source and then explaining how it supports your specific claim demonstrates:
o: Proper integration of evidence with commentary
quiz.e: Sources need commentary connecting them to the writer's own argument.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to select sources for the synthesis essay?
o: Choose sources that best support the specific argument you're making
Always use the first three sources listed
Avoid sources that could be used for a counterargument
quiz.e: Sources should be chosen strategically to support the writer's specific line of reasoning.

quiz.q: Citing sources by their letter (e.g., 'Source B') or clear paraphrase, rather than quoting at length, is generally:
o: Required to be verbatim quotes only
quiz.e: Concise citation paired with analysis is generally more effective than long unanalyzed quotes.

quiz.q: A synthesis essay that could be outlined using ONLY the writer's own claims (sources filling in support) is:
o: A sign of strong, argument-driven organization
A sign of a weak essay
quiz.e: This shows the essay is organized by argument, not merely summarizing sources.

quiz.q: Anticipating the strongest counterargument to your synthesis position and addressing it with a source is:
quiz.e: Addressing the strongest counterargument, supported by a source, strengthens the essay.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes synthesis from summary?
o: Synthesis develops the writer's OWN argument; summary just restates sources' content
quiz.e: Synthesis is argument-driven; summary is restatement without a governing claim.

quiz.q: Why is using FEWER than three sources a problem on the synthesis essay?
o: It fails to meet the minimum sourcing requirement of the task
quiz.e: At least three sources must be cited to meet the task's requirements.

quiz.q: A synthesis essay thesis that says 'Some believe X, others believe Y' without taking a position is:
quiz.e: A thesis must commit to a specific, defensible position, not just describe both sides.

quiz.q: Which best represents strategic sourcing to acknowledge a counterargument?
o: 'While Source C raises a valid concern about cost, the long-term benefits described in Source A outweigh it.'
'Source C says cost is a concern.'
Quoting Source C at full length with no commentary
quiz.e: This acknowledges the counterpoint, then explains why the writer's position still holds — using sources purposefully.

quiz.q: Why might a writer use a source they don't fully agree with in a synthesis essay?
o: To acknowledge and then rebut it as part of the argument
Sources you disagree with can never be cited
It's required to use all sources equally
quiz.e: Sources can be used to represent and then rebut opposing views.

quiz.q: A synthesis essay entirely organized as 'Source A, then Source B, then Source C' with no unifying claim across paragraphs is:
o: A structural weakness resembling a summary, not an argument
The best way to cite sources
quiz.e: This organization pattern fails to build a genuine, unified argument.

quiz.q: Which best reflects a synthesis essay's core goal?
o: Using sources as evidence to support the writer's own defensible claim
Reporting what each source states, in order
quiz.e: The synthesis essay's core goal is the writer's argument, supported by sources.

quiz.q: The rhetorical analysis essay primarily asks the writer to:
o: Explain HOW a writer builds their argument and its effect on the audience
Argue for or against the passage's topic
quiz.e: Rhetorical analysis focuses on HOW the argument is built, not whether the reader agrees with it.

quiz.q: The single most common error in rhetorical analysis essays is:
o: Arguing for or against the passage's topic instead of analyzing the writer's choices
quiz.e: Students often mistakenly argue the topic itself instead of analyzing HOW the writer argues.

quiz.q: A strong rhetorical analysis thesis should:
o: Identify the writer's purpose and preview the strategies to be analyzed
List every device in the passage
quiz.e: An effective thesis names purpose and previews the specific strategies discussed.

quiz.q: How many rhetorical strategies should a strong essay typically focus on?
quiz.e: A few well-developed strategies are stronger than many shallow ones.

quiz.q: 'This metaphor is used' without further explanation is an example of:
quiz.e: Quote-dropping — citing a device without explaining its effect — is a common weakness.

quiz.q: Which move should ALWAYS follow identifying a rhetorical device?
o: Explaining its specific effect on the audience
Moving to a new paragraph immediately
quiz.e: Device identification must be followed by an explanation of its effect.

quiz.q: Strategy-based essay structure means organizing body paragraphs by:
o: Each rhetorical strategy, traced through the whole passage
Each paragraph of the original passage, out of order
quiz.e: Strategy-based structure devotes each paragraph to tracing one strategy across the passage.

quiz.q: Chronological essay structure organizes body paragraphs by:
o: The passage's own order: beginning, middle, end
Only the strongest evidence, regardless of location
quiz.e: Chronological structure follows the passage's actual sequence.

quiz.q: Choosing strategies you can trace across MULTIPLE parts of a passage, rather than a single isolated line, is important because:
o: It supports a more developed, well-evidenced analysis
The exam requires only one example per device
quiz.e: Tracing a strategy across the passage allows for deeper, more convincing analysis.

quiz.q: Effects identified in rhetorical analysis should tie back to:
o: The writer's overall purpose established in the thesis
The reader's personal opinion of the topic
quiz.e: All analyzed effects should connect back to the overall purpose stated in the thesis.

quiz.q: Why should a rhetorical analysis essay start by identifying the rhetorical situation?
o: It grounds the analysis in speaker, audience, purpose, and occasion
Rhetorical situation only matters for synthesis essays
It replaces the need for a thesis
quiz.e: Establishing the rhetorical situation grounds the entire analysis that follows.

quiz.q: A rhetorical analysis essay that spends a whole paragraph arguing the topic is wrong (e.g., disagreeing with the writer's stance) is:
o: Off-task — this isn't what rhetorical analysis asks for
quiz.e: Arguing the topic itself, rather than analyzing the writer's rhetoric, is off-task.

quiz.q: Explaining WHY a specific word was chosen over an alternative demonstrates:
quiz.e: Explaining specific word choices over alternatives shows precise, strong analysis.

quiz.q: Which best completes a device-to-effect analysis: 'The anaphora of "we must"...'?
o: '...builds a mounting sense of urgency, compelling the audience toward collective action.'
quiz.e: This explains the specific effect on the audience, completing the device-to-effect move.

quiz.q: Each body paragraph in a rhetorical analysis essay needs its own:
o: Clear claim about a specific strategy's effect
quiz.e: Each paragraph should make its own specific claim about a strategy's effect.

quiz.q: Analyzing a persuasive speech, a student instead explains why they personally disagree with the speaker's cause. This essay:
o: Fails to fulfill the rhetorical analysis task
quiz.e: This confuses rhetorical analysis with an argument essay about the topic itself.

quiz.q: A rhetorical analysis thesis that only restates the passage's topic, without naming strategies or purpose, is:
quiz.e: A strong thesis must go beyond topic restatement to name purpose and strategies.

quiz.q: Which is a valid organizational approach for rhetorical analysis?
o: Either strategy-based or chronological structure, if reasoning is clear
Only strategy-based structure is ever acceptable
Only chronological structure is ever acceptable
quiz.e: Both structures are valid as long as the essay's reasoning is clear and well-organized.

quiz.q: Discussing 5+ rhetorical devices shallowly, with one sentence each, compared to 2-3 devices in depth, is generally:
o: A weaker approach than fewer, well-developed strategies
quiz.e: A few well-developed strategies produce stronger analysis than many shallow ones.

quiz.q: The argument essay primarily asks the writer to:
o: Develop and defend their own position using their own evidence
Cite at least three provided sources
quiz.e: Unlike synthesis or rhetorical analysis, the argument essay is entirely the writer's own claim and evidence.

quiz.q: Unlike the synthesis essay, the argument essay:
o: Provides no sources — evidence comes from the writer's own knowledge
quiz.e: The argument essay has no provided sources; the writer supplies their own evidence.

quiz.q: Which is considered valid evidence in an argument essay?
o: Historical examples, current events, literature, or personal experience
Only statistics from an official source packet
Nothing — the essay must be opinion only
quiz.e: A wide range of evidence types are valid, as long as they're specific and relevant.

quiz.q: One or two well-developed examples with real commentary is generally:
o: More persuasive than five examples mentioned only in passing
Weaker than a long list of brief examples
quiz.e: Depth of development matters more than sheer quantity of examples.

quiz.q: Restating the prompt itself as the thesis in an argument essay is:
o: A weakness — it isn't the writer's own specific, arguable position
quiz.e: A thesis must be the writer's own specific position, not a restatement of the prompt.

quiz.q: A 'qualified' thesis ('X is true, except when...') in an argument essay often demonstrates:
o: More sophisticated thinking than an absolute, all-or-nothing claim
quiz.e: Nuanced, qualified positions often show more sophisticated thinking than absolute claims.

quiz.q: Addressing a counterargument in the argument essay, then explaining why your position still holds, primarily demonstrates:
quiz.e: Engaging counterarguments shows awareness of complexity and strengthens the essay.

quiz.q: Which is an example of vague, unverifiable 'evidence' to avoid?
o: 'Studies show...' with no specific study named
A specific named historical event with details
A personal anecdote with concrete detail
A specific statistic with its source
quiz.e: Vague appeals to unnamed 'studies' lack the specificity of real evidence.

quiz.q: Explaining the broader implications or stakes of an argument is one way to demonstrate:
quiz.e: Broader implications/stakes are a recognized marker of sophisticated argumentation.

quiz.q: Vivid, effective writing style alone (without complex reasoning) is:
o: Not equivalent to sophistication — reasoning must also be genuinely complex
Sufficient by itself for sophistication credit
quiz.e: Sophistication requires substantive complexity of reasoning, not just polished prose.

quiz.q: Making nuanced distinctions ('this is true in some contexts but not others') shows:
quiz.e: Nuanced context-dependent claims demonstrate sophisticated thinking.

quiz.q: Ignoring the counterargument entirely in an argument essay tends to make the essay seem:
o: Incomplete or naive in its reasoning
quiz.e: Ignoring counterarguments weakens the perceived completeness of the reasoning.

quiz.q: Which best shows specific, well-developed evidence rather than a vague generality?
o: Detailing the 1969 moon landing's effect on public trust in science, with specifics
'Space exploration has helped society in many ways'
quiz.e: The specific, detailed example is far stronger than the vague general statements.

quiz.q: An argument essay may take which kind of position on the given claim?
o: Agree, disagree, or agree with qualifications — any defensible position
quiz.e: Any well-supported, defensible position is acceptable.

quiz.q: Why must argument-essay evidence be 'verifiably true or at least reasonably plausible'?
o: Fabricated evidence is always more persuasive
Only statistics need to be true
quiz.e: Invented or implausible 'facts' damage the writer's ethos/credibility.

quiz.q: A basic thesis-evidence-conclusion structure without further nuance is generally scored as:
o: Competent but not necessarily the most sophisticated approach
quiz.e: Basic structure can be competent, but sophistication requires going beyond it with nuance.

quiz.q: Which best reflects addressing complexity in an argument essay?
o: 'While exceptions exist in emergency situations, the general policy remains sound because...'
'This policy is always correct in every case.'
quiz.e: Acknowledging exceptions while still defending the general position shows nuanced, complex thinking.

quiz.q: In an argument essay, personal experience as evidence is:
o: A valid evidence source if specific and relevant
Only acceptable in the synthesis essay
quiz.e: Personal experience is valid evidence when specific and relevant to the claim.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes the argument essay from the synthesis essay?
o: The argument essay uses the writer's own evidence; synthesis requires citing provided sources
Argument essays require three sources, just like synthesis
Synthesis essays never require a thesis
quiz.e: This is the defining structural difference between the two essay types.

quiz.q: 'I went to the store, I bought milk' joined only by a comma is a:
quiz.e: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma is a comma splice.

quiz.q: 'Running quickly to the store.' with no subject or complete thought is a:
quiz.e: This lacks a complete subject-verb thought and cannot stand alone — a fragment.

quiz.q: 'I went to the store I bought milk' with no punctuation at all connecting the clauses is a:
quiz.e: Independent clauses joined with no punctuation or connector at all form a run-on.

quiz.q: The best fix for a comma splice is:
o: A period, semicolon, or coordinating conjunction
Removing the comma entirely with nothing else
quiz.e: Comma splices are fixed with a period, semicolon, or conjunction — not just removing the comma.

quiz.q: 'To run, jumping, and swim' violates:
quiz.e: The list mixes grammatical forms (infinitive, gerund, base verb) instead of matching them.

quiz.q: The corrected parallel version of 'to run, jumping, and swim' is:
o: To run, to jump, and to swim
To running, jumping, and to swim
quiz.e: All three items should share the same grammatical form — infinitives here.

quiz.q: 'The list of items are on the table' contains what error?
quiz.e: The singular subject 'list' requires the singular verb 'is,' not 'are.'

quiz.q: Which correctly demonstrates subject-verb agreement despite intervening words?
o: 'The box of old books is heavy.'
'The box of old books are heavy.'
'The boxes of old book is heavy.'
'The box of old book are heavy.'
quiz.e: 'Box' (singular) is the true subject, so it takes 'is,' regardless of the intervening 'of old books.'

quiz.q: A multiple-choice reading question asking for a passage's main claim tests:
o: Close reading of the passage's overall argument
Personal opinion, unrelated to the text
quiz.e: Main-claim questions test comprehension of the passage's overall argument.

quiz.q: When answering a reading multiple-choice question, you should always:
o: Go back to the passage to verify the answer
quiz.e: Verifying against the actual passage text is the most reliable strategy.

quiz.q: A 'half-right' wrong answer choice is one that is:
o: True in general but not actually supported by this specific passage
quiz.e: Distractors are often plausible-sounding but not supported by the specific passage.

quiz.q: A writing multiple-choice question asking for the 'best transition' tests:
o: Revision skill — choosing language that fits the passage's logic
quiz.e: Writing questions test a student's ability to revise for clarity, logic, and fit.

quiz.q: A question asking 'which choice best maintains the established tone' requires:
o: Checking the surrounding sentences' tone, not just grammar
Ignoring the rest of the passage
Choosing the most formal option automatically
quiz.e: Tone-matching questions require attention to the surrounding passage's tone.

quiz.q: A question asking which choice would be 'LEAST effective' requires:
o: Reading the question stem carefully — the correct answer is the WORST option
Choosing the best-written answer as usual
quiz.e: Some questions invert the usual logic and ask for the least effective/worst choice.

quiz.q: 'Everyone must bring their own laptop' mixing a singular antecedent ('everyone') with a plural pronoun ('their') is an example (in the strict formal usage tested) of:
quiz.e: 'Everyone' is singular, so strict formal usage pairs it with a singular pronoun form.

quiz.q: Fixing a comma splice by just deleting the comma with nothing else added typically creates:
o: A run-on sentence instead of a correct one
quiz.e: Removing only the comma, with no replacement punctuation, creates a run-on.

quiz.q: A question asking where to best place a sentence within a paragraph tests:
quiz.e: Placement questions test understanding of a paragraph's logical organization.

quiz.q: Which sentence demonstrates correct parallel structure?
o: 'She enjoys reading, to write, and hikes.'
'She enjoys to read, writing, and hike.'
'She enjoys reads, writing, and to hike.'
quiz.e: All three items share the same gerund ('-ing') form, making the structure parallel.

quiz.q: Why is it important to read the multiple-choice question stem carefully before answering?
o: Some questions ask for the least effective option or a deletion, reversing the usual logic
All questions ask for the best option, so stems never matter
Stems only matter for the reading section
quiz.e: Careful reading prevents missing inverted questions (e.g., 'least effective,' 'should be deleted').

quiz.q: A speaker who cites their own years of firsthand field experience is primarily building:
quiz.e: Firsthand experience/credentials build credibility — ethos.

quiz.q: 'The negotiations collapsed. Talks failed. Trust was gone.' uses short syntax primarily to create:
o: A blunt, emphatic sense of finality
Confusion about the sequence of events
quiz.e: The clipped, short sentences create emphasis and a sense of blunt finality.

quiz.q: Which best shows a synthesis essay citation properly paired with commentary?
o: 'Source A's data on wait times shows the current system is failing patients most in need.'
'According to Source A...' with no further explanation
Quoting Source A in full with no analysis
quiz.e: This pairs the citation with commentary explaining its significance to the argument.

quiz.q: Which best reflects analyzing a shift in strategy across a passage's structure?
o: The essay opens with logos-heavy statistics before pivoting to pathos-driven anecdotes in the closing paragraphs
Ignoring how the passage changes over its length
Treating the whole passage as using one unchanging strategy
quiz.e: Tracking how strategies shift across the passage shows sophisticated structural analysis.

quiz.q: Which best demonstrates addressing the 'stakes' of an argument for sophistication credit?
o: Explaining what could go wrong for real communities if the policy is NOT adopted
Simply restating the thesis a second time
quiz.e: Explaining real-world stakes/implications is a recognized way to show sophistication.

quiz.q: 'Neither the teacher nor the students was ready' should actually use which verb to agree with the nearer subject?
o: 'were,' agreeing with the nearer plural subject 'students'
quiz.e: With 'neither...nor,' the verb agrees with the subject closer to it — 'students' (plural) takes 'were.'

quiz.q: In the SOAPSTone framework, the 'S' that refers to the argument's central idea or message is:
quiz.e: SOAPSTone: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone.

quiz.q: 'Exigence' in a rhetorical situation is best defined as:
o: the urgent problem or issue that prompts the writer to respond
quiz.e: Exigence is the 'why now' - the situation that calls for discourse.

quiz.q: A speech delivered the day after a natural disaster, urging immediate aid, is a strong example of using:
quiz.e: Kairos is choosing the opportune moment and fitting the message to it.

quiz.q: Which is the best phrasing of a rhetorical PURPOSE?
o: to persuade skeptical voters that the policy will lower costs
the high cost of the policy
quiz.e: Purpose is a verb phrase: what the writer wants the audience to think, feel, or do.

quiz.q: 'Constraints' in a rhetorical situation refers to:
o: factors that limit how the writer can respond (beliefs, conventions, prior events)
the length limit of the essay
quiz.e: Constraints shape and restrict the available means of persuasion.

quiz.q: Analyzing 'audience' well on the exam means identifying:
o: the specific intended readers and their likely values and knowledge
anyone who might read the text
quiz.e: Audience analysis names the particular readers and what they need to be persuaded.

quiz.q: The rhetorical triangle connects the speaker, the audience, and the:
quiz.e: The three points correspond roughly to ethos, pathos, and logos.

quiz.q: A well-reasoned op-ed published years after the relevant debate has ended most clearly fails at:
quiz.e: It may be logically sound but misses the opportune moment and audience.

quiz.q: Occasion, in SOAPSTone, refers to:
o: the time, place, and circumstances that give rise to the text
quiz.e: Occasion is the immediate and larger context prompting the writing.

quiz.q: Which question best begins an audience analysis?
o: What does this audience already believe, and what would it take to move them?
What devices does the writer use?
quiz.e: Effective analysis starts from the audience's assumptions, values, and needs.

quiz.q: An appeal based on the speaker's character, expertise, and trustworthiness is:
quiz.e: Ethos is the appeal to credibility.

quiz.q: 'You can't trust her argument about the budget; she failed a math class in college' is an example of:
quiz.e: Ad hominem attacks the person rather than the argument.

quiz.q: Presenting only two options when more exist is the fallacy of:
quiz.e: A false dilemma forces a choice between two extremes.

quiz.q: Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack is:
quiz.e: The straw man refutes a distorted version of the argument.

quiz.q: Reasoning that moves from specific observations to a general conclusion is:
quiz.e: Induction builds a general claim from particular cases and is always provisional.

quiz.q: Which best completes strong rhetorical analysis of an emotional appeal?
o: name the words used, then explain the feeling they create and its effect on the audience
state that the author uses pathos
quiz.e: Always connect the specific language to the effect on the reader and the writer's purpose.

quiz.q: 'This policy must work; the senator who wrote it is very experienced' relies on:
o: an appeal to authority (which is weak if the authority is not relevant or is the only support)
quiz.e: Authority can support a claim, but it is a fallacy when the authority is irrelevant or offered as sole proof.

quiz.q: A writer who admits a personal mistake early in an essay is most likely trying to:
quiz.e: Acknowledging limits can build trust with the audience.

quiz.q: 'Post hoc, ergo propter hoc' is the fallacy of assuming that:
o: because one event followed another, the first caused the second
the majority opinion must be correct
a claim is true because it has not been disproven
an argument is sound because it is popular
quiz.e: It confuses sequence with causation.

quiz.q: The 'persona' a writer projects is:
o: the character the text creates through its language, tone, and stance
quiz.e: Persona is the version of the writer the reader perceives from the words on the page.

quiz.q: Repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses is:
quiz.e: Anaphora repeats at the START of clauses; epistrophe repeats at the end.

quiz.q: Placing contrasting ideas in parallel grammatical structure is:
quiz.e: 'Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country' is antithesis.

quiz.q: A direct comparison that does NOT use 'like' or 'as' is a:
quiz.e: A simile uses 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor states the comparison directly.

quiz.q: Deliberately omitting conjunctions from a list ('I came, I saw, I conquered') is:
quiz.e: Asyndeton speeds a list and can create urgency or breathlessness.

quiz.q: Repeating conjunctions in a series ('and this and this and this') is:
quiz.e: Polysyndeton slows a list and can add weight or a sense of accumulation.

quiz.q: A brief reference to a well-known person, event, or text is:
quiz.e: An allusion borrows meaning and feeling from a source the audience recognizes.

quiz.q: An extended metaphor is best described as:
o: a single comparison developed across several sentences or a whole passage
quiz.e: It structures a stretch of text around one governing comparison.

quiz.q: A rhetorical question is asked mainly to:
o: make a point or provoke thought rather than to get an answer
quiz.e: The answer is implied; the device engages the reader in the reasoning.

quiz.q: Verbal irony occurs when a writer:
o: says the opposite of what is meant, expecting the audience to catch the gap
quiz.e: Sarcasm is a common, pointed form of verbal irony.

quiz.q: After identifying anaphora in a passage, the next step in analysis is to:
o: explain the emphasis or momentum it builds and how that serves the purpose
quiz.e: Analysis must move from naming the device to explaining its effect.

quiz.q: 'Diction' refers to a writer's:
quiz.e: Diction is the specific words a writer selects, including their connotations.

quiz.q: The literal dictionary meaning of a word is its:
quiz.e: Connotation is the emotional or cultural association a word carries beyond its denotation.

quiz.q: 'Syntax' is:
o: the arrangement of words and phrases into sentences
quiz.e: Syntax includes sentence length, order, and structure.

quiz.q: Tone is best defined as:
o: the writer's attitude toward the subject or audience
quiz.e: Tone is the writer's stance; mood is the atmosphere the reader experiences.

quiz.q: A sudden shift from long, complex sentences to a short, blunt one usually functions to:
quiz.e: The abrupt change in rhythm draws attention to the short sentence's content.

quiz.q: Which is the most precise description of tone?
quiz.e: Precise tone words name a specific attitude rather than a vague quality.

quiz.q: A periodic sentence is one that:
o: withholds the main clause until the end
states the main clause first, then adds detail
quiz.e: Delaying the main idea builds suspense and emphasis.

quiz.q: Imagery is language that:
quiz.e: Imagery makes an idea vivid by engaging sight, sound, touch, taste, or smell.

quiz.q: A writer's selection of details is rhetorically significant because:
o: what a writer chooses to include or omit reveals a stance
quiz.e: Selection of detail is itself a form of argument.

quiz.q: A cumulative (loose) sentence:
o: begins with the main clause and adds modifying phrases after it
has two independent clauses joined by a semicolon
quiz.e: It leads with the core idea, then piles on detail.

quiz.q: A claim of policy argues that:
o: a specific action should or should not be taken
something is or is not true
a term should be defined a certain way
quiz.e: Claims of fact, value, and policy answer 'is it so?', 'is it good?', and 'what should we do?'

quiz.q: The difference between summary and commentary is that commentary:
o: explains HOW the evidence supports the claim
quiz.e: Commentary does the analytical work of connecting evidence to the argument.

quiz.q: A 'line of reasoning' is:
o: the logical progression connecting thesis, claims, and evidence
quiz.e: It is the through-line that makes an argument coherent.

quiz.q: Adding 'in most cases' to a claim is an example of:
quiz.e: Qualifiers narrow a claim to what the evidence can support.

quiz.q: Evidence is 'relevant' when it:
o: bears directly on the specific claim being made
quiz.e: Relevance is about fit with the exact claim, not about vividness or authority.

quiz.q: A single striking anecdote used to support a broad generalization is:
quiz.e: One story rarely proves a sweeping claim, even if it is on point.

quiz.q: A claim of value asserts that something is:
o: good or bad, better or worse, moral or immoral
quiz.e: Value claims involve judgment against a standard.

quiz.q: 'Cherry-picking' data is a problem of:
o: sufficiency and honesty (selecting only supportive evidence)
quiz.e: The evidence may be relevant but is incomplete and misleading.

quiz.q: Which sentence is commentary rather than summary?
o: This statistic matters because it shows the policy affects the very group it claims to help.
The author states that 40 percent of families were affected.
The author cites a government report.
quiz.e: Commentary interprets the evidence's significance for the argument.

quiz.q: A concession in an argument:
o: acknowledges that an opposing point has some merit
quiz.e: Concession builds credibility before the writer counters the point.

quiz.q: An effective thesis statement is:
quiz.e: A thesis someone could dispute, and that previews a line of reasoning, is strongest.

quiz.q: A topic sentence in a body paragraph should:
o: state the paragraph's sub-claim and connect to the thesis
restate the thesis word for word
quiz.e: It orients the reader to the paragraph's job in the argument.

quiz.q: The 'given-new' principle recommends that a sentence:
o: begin with familiar information and end with the new point
quiz.e: Leading with the known creates flow between sentences.

quiz.q: 'Concede-then-counter' means:
o: granting an opposing point, then explaining why it does not defeat the thesis
restating the opposing view sympathetically and stopping
quiz.e: It shows fairness, then limits the concession's force.

quiz.q: Transitions such as 'however' and 'therefore' should:
o: name the logical relationship between ideas
quiz.e: Misused transitions (e.g. 'however' with no contrast) confuse the reader.

quiz.q: Organizing an essay as problem-then-solution is a mode of:
quiz.e: Arrangement is the pattern by which material is ordered.

quiz.q: A conclusion is most effective when it:
o: extends the argument's significance rather than merely restating it
introduces a brand-new claim with no support
quiz.e: A strong conclusion answers 'so what?' and leaves the reader with the stakes.

quiz.q: 'Pointing words' like 'this' and 'such' require:
o: a clear referent so the reader knows what they refer to
quiz.e: Vague 'this' without a noun leaves the reader guessing.

quiz.q: Climactic (order-of-importance) arrangement means:
o: building from weaker points to the strongest
quiz.e: Ending on the strongest point leaves the reader with the best case.

quiz.q: Repeating a key term across paragraphs, rather than always finding synonyms, helps:
o: keep the argument's thread visible to the reader
quiz.e: Consistent key terms aid coherence more than 'elegant variation'.

quiz.q: The AP synthesis essay requires the writer to:
o: develop an argument that uses at least three of the provided sources as support
compare the sources to one another
choose the single best source and analyze it
quiz.e: Sources are evidence for the writer's own position, cited (at least three).

quiz.q: The 'summary trap' in a synthesis essay is:
o: walking through the sources one by one instead of organizing by your own claims
quiz.e: Body paragraphs should be built around sub-claims, drawing in sources as needed.

quiz.q: A 'defensible' thesis for a synthesis prompt is one that:
o: takes a clear, arguable position that the sources can be used to support
quiz.e: It should be specific and possible to argue against.

quiz.q: A signal phrase does which of the following?
o: names the source within the sentence introducing its idea
places the citation in parentheses at the end
quiz.e: 'Source B contends that...' is a signal phrase.

quiz.q: Sources that disagree with each other are:
o: useful, because one can be used to complicate or answer another
evidence that the prompt is flawed
quiz.e: Tension between sources can drive the argument forward.

quiz.q: In a synthesis essay, a quotation should generally be:
o: introduced and then explained, used only when the exact wording matters
quiz.e: Frame quotations and keep them short; paraphrase when wording is not the point.

quiz.q: Organizing a synthesis essay 'by your claims' means:
o: each body paragraph advances one of your sub-points, supported by whatever sources fit
paragraphs alternate pro and con sources
the essay follows the order the sources are printed
quiz.e: Your argument, not the source list, provides the structure.

quiz.q: A qualified synthesis thesis (e.g. 'Public financing helps in local races but less in national ones') is preferable because it:
o: is more precise and defensible than a sweeping claim
quiz.e: Nuance that the sources can support tends to score higher.

quiz.q: A rhetorical analysis essay asks the writer to explain:
o: HOW a writer makes an argument and to what effect
WHETHER the writer's argument is correct
quiz.e: Analysis focuses on rhetorical choices and their purpose, not on agreeing or disagreeing.

quiz.q: A weak rhetorical analysis thesis:
o: merely lists devices ('the author uses ethos, pathos, and logos')
states what the writer does and why
makes an arguable claim about the choices
quiz.e: A device list is not an argument about the passage.

quiz.q: 'Device-dropping' refers to:
o: naming a strategy and quoting a line without explaining its effect
quiz.e: Every identified choice must be tied to an effect on the audience and the purpose.

quiz.q: When a passage shifts in tone, the analysis should:
o: identify where and how the shift occurs and what it accomplishes
ignore it and label the whole passage with one tone
quiz.e: Tonal shifts usually mark a turn in the argument.

quiz.q: For a timed rhetorical analysis, the best approach to strategies is usually:
quiz.e: Depth of analysis beats breadth of identification.

quiz.q: A defensible rhetorical analysis thesis should be:
o: arguable - a reasonable reader could interpret the choices differently
a statement of fact everyone accepts
a personal opinion about the topic
quiz.e: It makes a claim about the writer's choices that requires support.

quiz.q: Analyzing the effect of a metaphor means explaining:
o: what understanding or feeling the comparison creates for the audience
the dictionary definition of the vehicle
quiz.e: Connect the figurative comparison to the writer's purpose.

quiz.q: A strong body paragraph in a rhetorical analysis essay:
o: identifies a choice, provides textual evidence, and explains the effect on the argument
quiz.e: Claim-evidence-analysis is the core structure.

quiz.q: The argument essay asks the writer to:
o: take and defend a position using their own reasoning and evidence
analyze how a given passage argues
quiz.e: It is the student's own argument, without provided sources.

quiz.q: For evidence in the argument essay, it is generally best to:
o: develop one or two examples thoroughly
list as many examples as possible
quiz.e: Depth of development and analysis matters more than quantity.

quiz.q: 'Sophistication' on the AP argument rubric can be earned by:
o: situating the argument in a broader context or acknowledging complexity
quiz.e: Nuance, tension, and a compelling style signal sophisticated thought.

quiz.q: Refutation differs from concession in that refutation:
o: directly answers an opposing argument and shows why it fails
grants that the opposing point has merit
quiz.e: Concession yields ground; refutation contests it.

quiz.q: A clear 'line of reasoning' in the argument essay means:
