That they are fleeing the village to escape a plague that has come upon the whole colony this year
That they are the ghosts of soldiers who died in a battle long ago and now walk in the dark forest
quiz.e: The devil promises knowledge of secret sin.

quiz.q: How does Brown treat the townspeople the next morning? (p. 67-68)
o: He shrinks from the minister, suspects Gookin's prayer, snatches a child from Goody Cloyse, and greets Faith sternly
He greets everyone warmly and tells them of his strange adventure in the forest during the night before
He preaches a sermon in the meeting-house about the need for repentance and a return to the church
He confesses everything to Faith and asks her forgiveness for leaving her alone on the night before
quiz.e: Hawthorne asks whether it was only a dream.

quiz.q: What does the last paragraph of “Young Goodman Brown” say about his tombstone? (p. 68)
o: They carved no hopeful verse upon it, for his dying hour was gloom
It bore a portrait of Brown, carved by a friend, and a line of praise
It carried the single word “Faith” in large letters over his name
It marked the grave of a cheerful and beloved man in the village
quiz.e: The line stresses the lasting effect of his experience.

quiz.q: What is Roderick Usher's reason, given to the narrator, for wanting to preserve Madeline's body for a fortnight? (p. 82)
o: The worldly reason concerns the nature of her disease and the remote family burying ground, though the narrator doubts it
She asked before her death to be buried at sea, according to an old family custom, and he wished to honor her
He planned to have her cremated after the fortnight, and had already sent for a priest to bless her ashes
He wanted to wait for a distant relative to arrive from across the ocean to attend the family funeral rites
quiz.e: The narrator distrusts the reason but does not oppose it.

quiz.q: On what night does the storm and the reading of the Mad Trist occur? (p. 85)
o: About the seventh or eighth night after Madeline is placed in the vault
On their very first night together in the mansion, after the long ride
On the day of Madeline's funeral, as the family gathered in the hall
A year after the entombment, when Roderick had grown very ill
quiz.e: The narrator cannot sleep and Roderick appears with a lamp.

quiz.q: What is the “Mad Trist” by Sir Launcelot Canning described as by the narrator? (p. 88)
o: An antique book with “uncouth and unimaginative prolixity”
A new best-selling romance in fashion that season in the capital
A collection of hymns sung in the Usher family chapel each week
A book of poems written by Roderick himself in his youth
quiz.e: The narrator reads it only as the only book at hand.

quiz.q: What does the narrator say Usher believed about the stones of the house? (p. 75)
o: That the arrangement of the stones and fungi gave them a kind of sentience
That the stones were haunted by the restless ghost of his mother
That the stones could be sold to pay off the family's many debts
That the stones had been carried from Egypt by an ancient ancestor
quiz.e: The belief in the sentience of vegetable and even inorganic things is linked to the house.

quiz.q: How does Baker's jay first react when the acorn falls into the hole? (p. 138)
o: He is paralyzed, his smile fades, and he says he didn't hear it fall
He flies away at once without looking back at the cabin
He laughs out loud at the size of the hole in the roof
He calls the other jays to come and see what he has found
quiz.e: He then studies the hole and drops more acorns.

quiz.q: What does the first jay swear he will do? (p. 139)
o: Fill the hole if it takes a hundred years
Destroy the cabin and everything in it, board by board
Fly south for the winter and never return to the mountains
Ask Baker for help in solving the mystery of the hole
quiz.e: "I'm d—d if I don't fill you, if it takes a hundred years!"

quiz.q: Why does the owl from Nova Scotia not laugh? (p. 141)
o: He couldn't see anything funny in it, and was disappointed about Yosemite too
He was asleep during the whole performance and heard nothing
He had never seen acorns and did not understand the joke at all
He was afraid of the crowd of jays and stayed quiet
quiz.e: Twain closes the tale with a dry joke.

quiz.q: What does Baker mean by “If a jay ain't human, he better take in his sign”? (p. 138)
o: Jays are so human-like that no one can deny it
Jays should start advertising their skills to the miners
Jays are dangerous and should not be trusted around people
Jays should leave the mining camps and live elsewhere
quiz.e: It is a folksy, humorous claim of anthropomorphic likeness.

hardQuiz.q: A columnist writes about a proposed law 'while the committee is still taking public comment this week.' The clause most directly establishes:
o: kairos - the timeliness that makes the argument worth making now
hardQuiz.e: It signals that the moment is opportune for influence, a kairos appeal.

hardQuiz.q: An essay opens by describing a bridge collapse, then pivots to infrastructure funding. The opening functions primarily as:
o: exigence - the concrete event that makes the argument urgent
hardQuiz.e: The collapse is the pressing problem that calls for the discourse.

hardQuiz.q: A writer addressing a skeptical business audience begins with tax data and cost projections rather than moral appeals. This choice best reflects:
o: audience analysis - matching the appeal to what these readers value
hardQuiz.e: The writer calibrates evidence to an audience that prizes financial reasoning.

hardQuiz.q: In a letter to constituents, a senator writes 'As someone who grew up in a mill town...' The phrase primarily builds:
o: ethos, by establishing shared background with the audience
hardQuiz.e: Claiming common ground and lived experience strengthens credibility with that audience.

hardQuiz.q: A speaker at a memorial adopts a slow, formal cadence and elevated diction. The stylistic choice is best explained by:
o: the occasion, which calls for solemnity
hardQuiz.e: Occasion shapes appropriate tone and register.

hardQuiz.q: Which revision best states a rhetorical purpose for analysis?
o: 'to convince wary parents that the curriculum change will not lower standards'
'parents who are wary of the change'
hardQuiz.e: Purpose is a verb phrase naming the intended effect on a specific audience.

hardQuiz.q: A writer notes that she must keep her op-ed under 700 words and avoid partisan labels to be published. These are examples of:
hardQuiz.e: Constraints are the limits within which the writer must work.

hardQuiz.q: A magazine essay assumes readers already accept that climate change is real and argues instead about which policies to adopt. This assumption reflects the writer's judgment about:
hardQuiz.e: The writer builds on shared premises rather than arguing from scratch.

hardQuiz.q: A public health official times a statement about vaccination to coincide with the start of flu season. This is an appeal to:
hardQuiz.e: Aligning the message with a moment when the audience is receptive is kairos.

hardQuiz.q: An analytical claim that a writer 'establishes urgency in the opening by pairing a specific recent event with a countdown to a vote' is strong mainly because it:
o: names both a choice and its effect rather than just labeling a device
is longer than a simple thesis
hardQuiz.e: It identifies the rhetorical move and the purpose it serves.

hardQuiz.q: 'Either we ban the app entirely, or we surrender our children's privacy.' This sentence commits which fallacy?
hardQuiz.e: It presents two extremes as the only options.

hardQuiz.q: 'We should keep the policy because it has always been our policy.' This is:
hardQuiz.e: The mere fact of being long-standing is offered as sufficient justification.

hardQuiz.q: A writer restates an opponent's nuanced position as 'they want no rules at all,' then attacks that. This is:
hardQuiz.e: The opponent's actual view is distorted into an easier target.

hardQuiz.q: 'Studies show that students who eat breakfast score higher, so the school should provide free breakfast.' The reasoning is primarily:
o: inductive, moving from data to a policy claim
hardQuiz.e: It generalizes from evidence to a recommended action.

hardQuiz.q: 'All mammals are warm-blooded; whales are mammals; therefore whales are warm-blooded.' This is:
hardQuiz.e: It applies a general premise to a specific case.

hardQuiz.q: An author argues that regulating social media is like regulating tobacco. The strength of this depends most on:
o: how similar the two cases actually are in the relevant respects
hardQuiz.e: An analogy is only as strong as the relevant similarity between the cases.

hardQuiz.q: A politician responds to a question about corruption by talking at length about job creation. This is:
o: a red herring - diverting attention from the issue
hardQuiz.e: The response changes the subject rather than addressing the question.

hardQuiz.q: 'This treatment must be safe; no one has proven it dangerous.' This is:
hardQuiz.e: Absence of disproof is treated as proof.

hardQuiz.q: A writer's tone becomes noticeably more measured and concessive in the paragraph addressing critics. This shift most likely functions to:
o: strengthen ethos by showing fairness before countering
hardQuiz.e: Appearing reasonable toward the opposition builds credibility.

hardQuiz.q: 'Nine out of ten dentists' is offered with no information about how the dentists were chosen. The appeal to logos is weak because the evidence may be:
hardQuiz.e: Without sampling detail, the statistic could be selective or biased.

hardQuiz.q: An essayist writes with self-deprecating humor about his early failures before making his case. The persona he constructs is best described as:
o: humble and relatable, which disarms the audience
hardQuiz.e: The projected self shapes how the audience receives the argument.

hardQuiz.q: 'Because it is complex, the tax code must be unfair.' This reasoning:
o: is a non sequitur - the conclusion does not follow from the premise
hardQuiz.e: Complexity does not entail unfairness; the inference is unsupported.

hardQuiz.q: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields...' The repeated opening clause is:
hardQuiz.e: Anaphora repeats a phrase at the start of successive clauses for cumulative force.

hardQuiz.q: 'Government of the people, by the people, for the people' most clearly uses:
o: parallelism and anaphora-like repetition to emphasize a unified idea
hardQuiz.e: The matched prepositional phrases stress the people's centrality.

hardQuiz.q: A writer describes a bureaucracy as 'a vast machine that grinds slowly, gears meshing, paper flowing endlessly through its chambers.' This is:
o: an extended metaphor structuring the reader's view of the institution
hardQuiz.e: The single machine comparison is developed across the sentence to shape perception.

hardQuiz.q: 'I came, I saw, I conquered' omits conjunctions to produce:
o: asyndeton, a clipped, forceful rhythm suggesting swift, decisive action
hardQuiz.e: Dropping 'and' quickens the pace and conveys efficiency.

hardQuiz.q: 'And the rain fell and the river rose and the fields flooded and the roads closed' uses:
o: polysyndeton to create a sense of relentless accumulation
hardQuiz.e: Repeated 'and' slows the reader and stacks up the consequences.

hardQuiz.q: A speaker refers to a modern political struggle as 'our generation's Valley Forge.' This allusion works by:
o: transferring the endurance and eventual triumph associated with Valley Forge to the present cause
hardQuiz.e: Allusion imports the emotional and historical weight of its source.

hardQuiz.q: A columnist asks, 'How many more reports must we ignore before we act?' The rhetorical question functions to:
o: press the audience toward the conclusion that action is overdue
hardQuiz.e: The implied answer ('none more') advances the argument.

hardQuiz.q: 'It was not a small setback' is an example of:
o: litotes - understatement by negation, which can add dry emphasis
hardQuiz.e: Litotes affirms by denying the contrary, often with an ironic or measured effect.

hardQuiz.q: A writer calls a corporate apology 'a masterclass in saying sorry without meaning it.' The device is:
o: verbal irony (sarcasm), which conveys criticism through apparent praise
hardQuiz.e: The literal praise signals its opposite to the reader.

hardQuiz.q: 'Not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more' uses:
o: antithesis - contrasting ideas in parallel structure
hardQuiz.e: The balanced clauses set 'loved Caesar less' against 'loved Rome more'.

hardQuiz.q: After naming a passage's use of alliteration, the analysis is incomplete until it explains:
o: how the sound pattern draws attention to those words and supports the tone or point
the dictionary meaning of each word
hardQuiz.e: Device identification must be followed by analysis of effect.

hardQuiz.q: A writer describing a politician chooses words like 'shrewd,' 'calculating,' and 'relentless.' The diction primarily conveys:
o: a wary, somewhat critical attitude toward the subject
hardQuiz.e: Connotations of the word choices shape the reader's judgment.

hardQuiz.q: A paragraph of long, clause-heavy sentences is followed by: 'It failed.' The syntactic contrast functions to:
o: deliver the conclusion with blunt emphasis after elaborate build-up
hardQuiz.e: The short sentence lands harder because of what precedes it.

hardQuiz.q: A memoirist writes: 'The kitchen, small and yellow, its window fogged with steam, its table scarred by decades of homework and spilled coffee...' This cumulative sentence:
o: leads with the main image, then piles on modifying detail to build a rich impression
withholds the main clause for suspense
hardQuiz.e: A loose/cumulative sentence states the core first and accumulates description.

hardQuiz.q: 'Only after the votes were counted, the challenges dismissed, and the concession delivered did the result feel real.' This periodic sentence:
o: delays the main clause to build suspense and emphasize the moment of finality
hardQuiz.e: The main clause ('did the result feel real') arrives last.

hardQuiz.q: A writer's tone toward a new technology is best labeled:
hardQuiz.e: Precise tone words name a specific attitude, not a vague quality.

hardQuiz.q: An author describing urban decay lingers on 'boarded windows,' 'weeds in the sidewalk cracks,' and 'a single working streetlight.' The selection of detail:
o: builds an argument about neglect without stating it outright
is random and carries no meaning
hardQuiz.e: Choosing what to show is itself persuasive.

hardQuiz.q: A passage shifts from first person ('I remember') to second person ('you would have seen'). The shift in point of view most likely aims to:
o: draw the reader into the scene and generalize the experience
hardQuiz.e: Addressing 'you' invites the reader to share the writer's perspective.

hardQuiz.q: A writer repeatedly uses hedging phrases ('perhaps,' 'it may be,' 'one could argue'). The cumulative effect on tone is:
hardQuiz.e: Consistent hedging signals caution and open-endedness.

hardQuiz.q: 'Denotation' and 'connotation' differ in that connotation involves:
o: the associations and emotional coloring a word carries
hardQuiz.e: Two words with the same denotation (e.g. 'thrifty' vs. 'stingy') can carry opposite connotations.

hardQuiz.q: Choosing 'crowd' in one sentence and 'mob' in the next, for the same group, signals:
o: a deliberate shift in the writer's attitude toward the group
hardQuiz.e: The connotative jump from neutral to threatening is a rhetorical move.

hardQuiz.q: 'The city should expand bus service' is a claim of:
hardQuiz.e: It advocates a specific action.

hardQuiz.q: 'The current bus system leaves 40 percent of residents more than a mile from a stop' is a claim of:
hardQuiz.e: It asserts something verifiably true or false.

hardQuiz.q: Which sentence is commentary, not summary?
o: That gap matters because the underserved areas are exactly where car ownership is lowest.
The report says 40 percent of residents live far from a stop.
The passage cites a transit study.
hardQuiz.e: Commentary explains the significance of the evidence for the claim.

hardQuiz.q: A student writes: 'Public libraries are essential. They have books, computers, and meeting rooms.' The main weakness is:
o: the support lists features but never connects them to why libraries are essential
there is no evidence at all
hardQuiz.e: The evidence is not developed into reasoning that proves the claim.

hardQuiz.q: Adding 'in cities with existing rail infrastructure' to a claim about transit funding is an example of:
o: qualifying the claim to fit the evidence
hardQuiz.e: The qualifier limits the claim's scope to where support is strong.

hardQuiz.q: A writer supports a broad claim about teen reading habits with one interview of a single student. The evidence is best described as:
hardQuiz.e: One case cannot establish a general trend.

hardQuiz.q: 'This policy is unjust' is a claim of:
hardQuiz.e: It renders a moral judgment.

hardQuiz.q: A 'line of reasoning' is visible in an essay when:
o: each paragraph's point clearly follows from the last and builds toward the thesis
hardQuiz.e: It is the logical spine connecting claims and evidence.

hardQuiz.q: An author presents survey results but omits that the survey was conducted only among the policy's supporters. This is a failure of:
o: sufficiency and fairness (the sample is biased)
hardQuiz.e: The evidence is skewed and therefore inadequate to support a general claim.

hardQuiz.q: Which is the strongest commentary sentence after quoting a statistic about wage growth?
o: The figure undercuts the claim of broad prosperity because it excludes part-time workers, who make up most of the low-wage group.
The author provides a statistic about wage growth.
Wage growth is an important economic measure.
This is the second statistic in the passage.
hardQuiz.e: It interprets what the statistic means for the argument and notes a limitation.

hardQuiz.q: Which is the most effective thesis for an argument about a phone ban in schools?
o: A daytime phone ban improves focus, but schools must pair it with clear emergency procedures to earn parents' trust.
Phones are a big issue in schools today.
This essay will discuss phones in schools.
hardQuiz.e: It is specific, arguable, and previews a qualified line of reasoning.

hardQuiz.q: A body paragraph that opens by restating the thesis verbatim most likely:
o: fails to advance a distinct sub-claim
hardQuiz.e: Each paragraph should make its own point in service of the thesis.

hardQuiz.q: 'Critics worry about equity. That concern is fair: rural students may lack home internet. But the district's loaner program addresses it directly.' This sequence is:
hardQuiz.e: It grants the point, then limits its force.

hardQuiz.q: A paragraph begins each sentence with new, unexplained information and never links back to prior sentences. The likely problem is:
o: weak coherence - it violates the given-new pattern
hardQuiz.e: Readers lose the thread when sentences do not connect known to new.

hardQuiz.q: An essay is organized: history of the problem, current situation, proposed fix. This is primarily:
o: a problem-solution arrangement with a chronological lead-in
hardQuiz.e: The structure names a problem and argues toward a response.

hardQuiz.q: The transition 'however' is misused when it:
o: connects two statements that do not actually contrast
links a cause to an effect
hardQuiz.e: Transitions must accurately name the logical relationship.

hardQuiz.q: A conclusion that only restates the introduction in new words:
o: misses the chance to extend the argument's significance
is ideal for a timed essay
hardQuiz.e: A strong close answers 'so what?' and conveys the stakes.

hardQuiz.q: 'This raises a further question' is unclear if:
o: 'this' has no clear referent in the preceding sentences
it is followed by a question
hardQuiz.e: Pointing words need an unambiguous antecedent.

hardQuiz.q: Arranging supporting points from least to most persuasive uses:
o: climactic order, so the essay ends on its strongest note
hardQuiz.e: Building to the strongest point leaves the reader with the best case.

hardQuiz.q: Repeating the phrase 'shared responsibility' in each body paragraph of an argument essay most likely serves to:
o: keep the unifying idea visible and reinforce coherence
hardQuiz.e: Consistent key terms thread the argument together.

hardQuiz.q: A synthesis essay that devotes one paragraph each to summarizing Source A, then B, then C, then states an opinion, has fallen into:
o: the summary trap - it does not organize around the writer's own claims
hardQuiz.e: Synthesis must subordinate sources to the writer's line of reasoning.

hardQuiz.q: Two sources on museum funding disagree. The best synthesis move is to:
o: use one source to complicate or answer the other within a paragraph built on your claim
pick the source you like and ignore the other
summarize both and let the reader decide
note that they disagree and move on
hardQuiz.e: Disagreement between sources can advance your argument.

hardQuiz.q: 'Source C notes that attendance rose 20 percent after admission fees were dropped' is an example of:
o: a signal phrase integrating the source into the sentence
hardQuiz.e: The source is named within the sentence that presents its idea.

hardQuiz.q: A defensible synthesis thesis on a curfew prompt might be:
o: Curfews can reduce certain nighttime offenses, but only when paired with youth programs that address the underlying causes.
This essay examines several sources on curfews.
hardQuiz.e: It stakes an arguable, qualified position the sources can support.

hardQuiz.q: In a synthesis essay, dropping in a long quotation with no introduction or follow-up analysis:
o: weakens the paragraph because the source is not doing visible work in the argument
is acceptable if the quotation is from a strong source
hardQuiz.e: Quotations must be framed and explained.

hardQuiz.q: Organizing a synthesis essay 'by your claims' means each body paragraph:
o: advances one of your sub-points, bringing in whichever sources support it
follows the order the sources appear in the packet
hardQuiz.e: Your argument provides the structure; sources are evidence.

hardQuiz.q: The AP synthesis prompt's requirement to cite at least three sources means:
o: at least three of the provided sources must be used as evidence in the argument
the essay must have three body paragraphs
hardQuiz.e: Three or more sources must genuinely support the writer's claims.

hardQuiz.q: A synthesis body paragraph that uses Source A for a statistic, then Source D to explain a cause behind it, demonstrates:
o: sources working together to build one of the writer's points
hardQuiz.e: Combining sources to support a single claim is effective synthesis.

hardQuiz.q: A rhetorical analysis thesis that reads 'Douglass uses ethos, pathos, and logos to argue against slavery' is weak because it:
o: lists appeals without claiming what Douglass does or to what effect
hardQuiz.e: It is a checklist, not an arguable claim about the rhetorical strategy.

hardQuiz.q: A stronger version of that thesis would:
o: state how Douglass builds authority and moral urgency to make complacency untenable for his audience
hardQuiz.e: It names the moves and the intended effect on the audience.

hardQuiz.q: In analyzing a passage, writing 'The author uses a metaphor: "a river of debt."' and moving on is:
o: device-dropping - it lacks analysis of the metaphor's effect
hardQuiz.e: The analysis must explain what the comparison does for the argument.

hardQuiz.q: A passage moves from a somber recounting of losses to a determined call for reform. The best analytical move is to:
o: identify the tonal shift and explain how it repositions the audience from grief toward action
ignore the shift as a distraction
hardQuiz.e: Tonal shifts usually mark a turn in the argument's strategy.

hardQuiz.q: For a 40-minute rhetorical analysis essay, a student who identifies eight devices in the introduction and analyzes none in depth will most likely:
o: score lower than a student who analyzes three choices thoroughly
fail to address the prompt entirely
hardQuiz.e: The rubric rewards developed analysis over lists.

hardQuiz.q: A defensible claim about a writer's choice is one that:
o: a reasonable reader could dispute and that requires textual support
restates an obvious fact about the passage
expresses the analyst's opinion of the topic
hardQuiz.e: Analysis makes an arguable claim about how the text works.

hardQuiz.q: Analyzing the effect of short, declarative sentences in a passage means explaining that they:
o: create emphasis, urgency, or certainty appropriate to the writer's purpose
hardQuiz.e: Connect the syntactic pattern to the rhetorical effect.

hardQuiz.q: A body paragraph in a rhetorical analysis that quotes the passage but never explains the quotation's function:
o: provides evidence without analysis, the most common weakness
hardQuiz.e: Claim-evidence-analysis all need to be present.

hardQuiz.q: An argument essay that offers eight brief historical examples with a sentence each will most likely:
o: score lower than one that develops two examples with analysis
hardQuiz.e: Development and reasoning outweigh the number of examples.

hardQuiz.q: The clearest sign of a strong 'line of reasoning' in an argument essay is that:
o: each paragraph visibly advances the thesis in a logical order
the essay has an introduction and conclusion
the prompt is restated in each paragraph
hardQuiz.e: The reader can trace how the argument builds.

hardQuiz.q: 'While stricter licensing would inconvenience some hobbyists, the safety gains for the public outweigh that cost.' This sentence:
o: concedes a point, then counters it, strengthening the writer's ethos
hardQuiz.e: Concede-then-counter shows fairness before limiting the concession.

hardQuiz.q: Refutation in an argument essay:
o: directly answers an opposing argument and explains why it fails
grants that the opposing view is partly right
summarizes the opposing view without responding
is the same as a concession
hardQuiz.e: Refutation contests the opposing claim rather than yielding to it.

hardQuiz.q: A thesis such as 'Standardized tests measure some skills well but distort teaching when overused' is preferable to 'Standardized tests are bad' because it:
o: is nuanced and defensible, supporting a stronger line of reasoning
hardQuiz.e: Qualified, specific claims support better argumentation and can earn sophistication.

hardQuiz.q: 'Sophistication' on the AP rubric is most likely earned by:
o: placing the argument in a broader context or grappling with its complications
hardQuiz.e: Nuance, tension, and a compelling 'so what' signal sophisticated thought.

hardQuiz.q: Ending an argument essay with 'Ultimately, how we regulate this technology will shape what kind of public square we have' is effective because it:
o: answers 'so what?' by naming the larger stakes
introduces a new claim needing support
restates the thesis word for word
hardQuiz.e: A strong conclusion conveys why the argument matters.

hardQuiz.q: A writer who anticipates the strongest objection and answers it before the reader raises it is:
o: strengthening the argument by pre-empting refutation
hardQuiz.e: Addressing the best counterargument builds credibility and a tighter case.

hardQuiz.q: Which sentence contains a comma splice?
o: The evidence was thin, the conclusion was bold.
The evidence was thin, but the conclusion was bold.
Although the evidence was thin, the conclusion was bold.
The evidence was thin; the conclusion was bold.
hardQuiz.e: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma is a splice.

hardQuiz.q: Which choice corrects 'She enjoys reading, to write, and painting.'?
o: She enjoys reading, writing, and painting.
She enjoys to read, to write, and to paint, all of them.
She enjoys reading and to write and painting.
She enjoys reading, writing, and to paint.
hardQuiz.e: Parallel structure requires the items to match in form.

hardQuiz.q: 'The panel published its findings' is correct because 'panel' is:
o: a collective noun treated as singular in formal American usage
hardQuiz.e: Collective nouns take singular verbs and pronouns in standard American English when acting as a unit.

hardQuiz.q: Which uses a colon correctly?
o: The recipe needs three things: flour, water, and salt.
The recipe needs: flour, water, and salt.
The recipe needs three things; flour, water, and salt.
The recipe: needs flour, water, and salt.
hardQuiz.e: A colon follows a complete independent clause and introduces the list.

hardQuiz.q: On an MC revision item, the answer 'in the event that' should usually be replaced with:
o: 'in cases where it may be that'
hardQuiz.e: Concise diction is preferred; 'if' does the work.

hardQuiz.q: Which is the most concise version?
o: The committee is going to be holding a vote tomorrow.
A vote will be held by the committee on the day of tomorrow.
It is expected that a vote will be conducted tomorrow by the committee.
hardQuiz.e: The shortest option that preserves meaning is best.

hardQuiz.q: A semicolon is used correctly in:
o: The trial ended; the verdict surprised no one.
The trial ended; and the verdict surprised no one.
The trial ended; a swift verdict.
The trial ended; because the evidence was clear.
hardQuiz.e: A semicolon joins two independent clauses without a conjunction.

hardQuiz.q: On an MC reading question, if two answers seem plausible, the best tiebreaker is to:
o: check each against the exact wording and context of the passage
choose the one that matches common knowledge
hardQuiz.e: The correct answer must be supported by the text itself.

hardQuiz.q: 'The reason the plan failed is because the funding fell through' should be revised to:
o: The plan failed because the funding fell through.
The reason for the plan's failure is because of funding.
The plan failed due to the reason that funding fell through.
Because of the reason of funding, the plan failed.
hardQuiz.e: 'The reason ... is because' is redundant; use 'because' alone.

hardQuiz.q: Which sentence best fixes the dangling modifier in 'Walking into the room, the tension was obvious.'?
o: Walking into the room, I felt the tension immediately.
Walking into the room, the tension that was there was obvious.
The tension, walking into the room, was obvious.
Obvious was the tension walking into the room.
hardQuiz.e: The modifier must attach to a person who can walk, not to 'the tension'.

hardQuiz.q: A student writes: 'Poe's "vacant eye-like windows" show anthropomorphism.' What is the best correction?
o: It is personification, because the house is an inanimate object
It is anthropomorphism, because windows are living parts of a house
It is a simile, because it compares windows to eyes using the word “like”
It is dialect, because it reflects the speech of the region
hardQuiz.e: Anthropomorphism gives living beings (animals) human traits; personification gives objects human traits.

hardQuiz.q: Which best explains why the "Haunted Palace" poem matters to Usher's plot?
o: It allegorically previews Roderick's mental collapse and the house's fall
It proves that the narrator has been lying about what he really saw
It moves the story to a new setting that explains the ending
It provides a joke that lightens the gloomy mood for the reader
hardQuiz.e: The palace once ruled by Thought overrun by evil parallels Roderick's mind and the family's ruin.

hardQuiz.q: How does the "Mad Trist" scene function as foreshadowing?
o: The noises described in the romance echo sounds that reveal Madeline's return
It states the ending of the story outright before it actually happens
It introduces Roderick's parents and the family's dark old secrets
It describes the tarn and the fissure in the house's front wall
hardQuiz.e: Sounds in the tale coincide with real sounds, foreshadowing the climax.

hardQuiz.q: Which claim best states Twain's likely purpose in "Baker's Bluejay Yarn"?
o: To use a comic animal tale to poke fun at human foolishness and pride
To teach readers how to train and care for wild birds in the mountains
To honor the soldiers of the Union army after the war ended
To record the climate and the weather of California mining country
hardQuiz.e: Anthropomorphized jays mirror human behavior, so the humor works as social commentary.

hardQuiz.q: What makes Baker's dialect an effective indirect characterization?
o: His speech patterns and confident exaggeration reveal a folksy, sincere, tall-tale-telling personality
It tells readers his exact age, his birthplace and a good deal about his life before he came to the mines
It gives a full biography of his years in the East, before he came west to live alone in the mountains
It proves that he is really a bluejay in disguise, telling the story of his own kind in a human voice
hardQuiz.e: Indirect characterization works through speech and behavior.

hardQuiz.q: Which pairing correctly matches an allusion in "Young Goodman Brown" with its effect?
o: The serpent-like staff alluding to the serpent in Eden; it marks the traveler as the devil and raises the moral stakes
The pink ribbons alluding to a Greek myth; it shows the story is set in ancient Athens and long ago and far away
The forest alluding to a Shakespeare play; it makes the story a comedy and lightens the mood for the audience
The minister alluding to Mark Twain; it shows the year in which the story was actually written and printed
hardQuiz.e: The staff is a Biblical allusion tied to evil and temptation.

hardQuiz.q: Which statement best captures Hawthorne's take on the Puritans in this story?
o: Their public piety hides hypocrisy and harshness, and doubt can poison a whole life
They were the perfect model of virtue for every later generation
They were carefree and adventurous people who loved a good story
They were concerned mainly with trade and the price of goods in town
hardQuiz.e: Everyone Brown respects appears at the forest meeting, and Brown's life becomes bleak afterward.

hardQuiz.q: Why is the ambiguity (dream or reality?) important to the theme of "Young Goodman Brown"?
o: It shows that suspicion alone can destroy trust, whether or not the events were real
It proves that Brown made everything up in order to win attention
It turns the story into a comedy about a foolish and frightened husband
It is a printing error that later editors of the story corrected
hardQuiz.e: Brown's changed life matters more than whether the evidence was real.

hardQuiz.q: Which claim about "Rip Van Winkle" combines characterization and time period effectively?
o: Rip's easygoing idleness and the changed village let Irving suggest the new nation has traded a gentle old order for noisy politics
Rip is a scientist who studies the geology of the mountains he climbs, and finds that his research has gone out of date
Rip is a soldier who wins a battle in the war and is rewarded with a large farm in the valley for his bravery
Rip discovers gold in the mountains and returns to a village that has changed around him, richer than anyone there
hardQuiz.e: Tie characterization to the time change to state a purpose.

hardQuiz.q: Which is the strongest topic sentence for a paragraph on Irving's characterization of Dame Van Winkle?
o: Irving's harsh diction like "termagant" and "virago" leads readers to sympathize with Rip and to see Dame as an obstacle.
Dame Van Winkle is a character who appears often in Irving's story about the mountains and the village below them.
In the story, Irving includes a wife for the main character, a man named Rip who lives in the Hudson valley.
Irving wrote the story in England in 1819 while he was visiting his relatives there and working on new sketches.
hardQuiz.e: A strong claim names the device, the language, and the effect on the reader.

hardQuiz.q: A response to "The Eve of St. Agnes" says the cold opening and cold closing make the lovers' warmth feel fragile. This is analysis of:
o: Mood built through imagery and structure
Dialect spelling used to show the region of the speakers
A rhetorical fallacy that weakens the poem's argument
An allusion to a story by Mark Twain
hardQuiz.e: Cold-to-warm-to-cold framing shapes the reader's feeling.

hardQuiz.q: Emerson's materialist versus transcendentalist contrast is most useful for connecting to which story theme?
o: Individual intuition and imagination versus social facts and circumstances
The weather of New England and its effect on the crops of local farmers
The history of clocks and their role in the growth of industry
The costume design and dress of the Puritan settlers in Salem
hardQuiz.e: It ties directly to Romantic and Transcendental ideas about the mind.

hardQuiz.q: A student summarizes: 'Poe uses the House of Usher to show...' Which finishes the claim with analysis rather than plot?
o: …how a decaying mansion, described in gloomy imagery, mirrors and magnifies the collapse of Roderick's mind
…what happens on each page as the narrator rides up to the house, goes in and meets his friend Roderick
…that a man visits an old friend during the autumn and stays with him for some days in a lonely house
…that there was a fall of some kind at the end of the story and that the house was badly damaged by it
hardQuiz.e: Analysis links a device to meaning.

hardQuiz.q: Which pairing of author and dominant tone is most defensible for the Unit 1 selections?
o: Twain: humorous and satirical; Poe: dark and Gothic
Twain: solemn and preachy; Poe: light and playful
Twain: Gothic and ominous; Poe: comic and cheerful
Twain: mournful and grave; Poe: warm and cheerful
hardQuiz.e: Twain's yarn is comic and mocking; Poe's story is Gothic and ominous.

hardQuiz.q: Which thesis about “Rip Van Winkle” best combines characterization and historical context?
o: Irving's affectionate portrait of an idle, henpecked Rip against a village transformed by the Revolution suggests a nation changing faster than its people can follow
Rip Van Winkle is a story about a man who sleeps for a very long time in the woods and wakes up an older man and a bit confused about it
Irving wrote about the Revolution because he was born during it and named for Washington, and he wanted to honor the general in his writing
Dame Van Winkle is the more admirable and hard-working character in the story, and Irving means for readers to side with her against her husband
hardQuiz.e: A strong thesis names devices and purpose; the wrong choices are summary or trivia.

hardQuiz.q: Which line from Baker's yarn best supports the claim that the jay behaves like a frustrated human?
o: “Then he begun to get mad ... and he broke loose and cussed himself black in the face.”
“Animals talk to each other, of course. There can be no question about that.”
“He was a middle-aged, simple-hearted miner who had lived in a lonely corner.”
“There stands his house, been empty ever since; a log house with a plank roof.”
hardQuiz.e: The jay's anger and swearing are the clearest human behavior.

hardQuiz.q: Which explains why Twain's use of Baker's voice makes the tall tale funnier?
o: Baker's earnest, dialect-heavy certainty contrasts with the ridiculous story, so the reader laughs at both the jay and the teller
Baker openly announces at the start of his tale that it is only a joke to be enjoyed, so readers know when to laugh at it
Baker uses formal academic language that makes the story sound scientific and true, so the humor comes from its careful proof
Baker refuses to describe the jay's feelings, leaving the readers to guess what he feels, and so the story is left a mystery
hardQuiz.e: Juxtaposition of a serious tone and a silly tale creates humor.

hardQuiz.q: In “Young Goodman Brown”, the traveler says the governor and the deacons "have drunk the communion wine with me". This detail most strongly develops which idea?
o: Evil and hypocrisy are hidden within respected Puritan leaders
The traveler is a wine merchant who sells to the churches in the region
The Puritans of New England have an extensive network of trade and business
Brown has a poor memory and cannot recall who his neighbors and friends are
hardQuiz.e: It suggests the whole community is corrupted.

hardQuiz.q: Brown's wife is named Faith and he cries “My Faith is gone!” This double meaning is an example of
o: Wordplay that turns a person into a symbol of religious belief
Onomatopoeia that imitates the sound of a person's voice
Foreshadowing of a wedding that will take place later
Dialect spelling that shows how Salem villagers spoke
hardQuiz.e: "Faith" refers to both his wife and his belief.

hardQuiz.q: Which explains how “The Haunted Palace” functions in Usher?
o: It is an allegory in which the palace stands for Roderick's mind, previewing its ruin
It is a song about a real castle that once stood beside the tarn
It is a comic interlude that lightens the story's gloomy mood for readers
It reveals the narrator's own family history and its hidden secrets
hardQuiz.e: The palace once ruled by Thought overrun by evil parallels Roderick's mental collapse.

hardQuiz.q: Which best explains why Poe includes the Mad Trist read aloud by the narrator?
o: The sounds it describes seem to echo and cause events in the house, heightening suspense and blurring fiction and reality
It introduces a new setting that carries the story on to its ending after the storm has passed over the old house
It corrects Roderick's mistaken belief about the tarn and the cracked walls of the house that he has feared for years
It reveals that the narrator wrote the entire story himself as a private diary of his stay in a lonely house by the tarn
hardQuiz.e: The inset romance builds the climax.

hardQuiz.q: Which explains the effect of Keats's Spenserian stanza with its longer final line?
o: The extended last line slows the rhythm and gives each stanza a sense of closure or emphasis
The extended last line turns the whole poem into a comedy with a comic ending
The extended last line removes the need for vivid imagery in each stanza
The extended last line shows that the speaker is angry with the lovers
hardQuiz.e: The final alexandrine adds weight.

hardQuiz.q: A student claims, “Keats uses cold imagery at the beginning and end to show that love is fragile against time and death.” Which evidence best supports this?
o: The Beadsman's frozen breath at the start and his sleeping “among his ashes cold” at the end
The names of the lovers, Madeline and Porphyro, and their family feud at the start of the poem
The description of the feast's fruits and sweets laid out in the warm chamber for Madeline
The lute's Provencal song that wakes Madeline in the middle of the night before the flight
hardQuiz.e: Cold bookends the warm love story.

hardQuiz.q: Which claim about Emerson's excerpt is best supported by the text?
o: It presents the idealist as valuing consciousness over society, government, labor and property except as symbols of truth
It says that government is the highest good that a person can serve in this world, above every other duty and desire
It says nothing about consciousness and focuses only on the beauty of nature and the changes of the seasons in the country
It praises luxury and social art above every other value that a person can hold, and treats the mind as a lesser thing
hardQuiz.e: The idealist "does not respect labor ... property" otherwise than as a symbol.

hardQuiz.q: How does Adams' phrase “regardless of the fortuitous circumstances of birth or position” shape his definition of the American Dream?
o: It stresses equality of opportunity based on ability, not on family status
It makes the dream depend mostly on luck and chance, not on effort
It excludes people who lack money or education from the promise of the dream
It equates the dream with the special privileges of an aristocracy
hardQuiz.e: Fortuitous means by chance; birth and position should not decide a person's fate.

hardQuiz.q: Which BEST distinguishes anthropomorphism from personification using two examples from the unit?
o: Baker's talking bluejays are anthropomorphism (living creatures); Usher's “eye-like windows” are personification (an object)
Baker's jays are personification (a bird as a person); Usher's windows are anthropomorphism (a thing as a person)
Both the jays and the windows are examples of anthropomorphism, as both are given human traits by their authors
Both the jays and the windows are examples of personification, as both are things of nature that seem to act like people
hardQuiz.e: The class schedule definitions: anthropomorphism for animate beings; personification for inanimate objects.

hardQuiz.q: Which best explains the effect of Irving's historical frame (Diedrich Knickerbocker's papers)?
o: It adds a playful, faux-historical authority that invites readers to enjoy the tale while smiling at the idea of history
It proves that the story is nonfiction taken from real historical records kept by the Dutch settlers of the valley
It removes the need for any narrator to tell the story to the reader, since the papers speak for themselves
It warns readers to avoid fantasy and to stay with facts about the past, since fiction cannot teach the truth
hardQuiz.e: The fake historian frame is part of Irving's satire.

hardQuiz.q: Which sentence best states the purpose of Hawthorne's Salem forest setting?
o: The darkness and unknown woods symbolize moral testing, where hidden sin can be seen and trust is lost
The forest is simply a place where the villagers of Salem go to hunt for game and to gather firewood in the fall
The forest proves that Brown is an experienced woodsman who knows every path and hidden trail in the whole colony
The forest shows the trade routes that the colony used to reach the coast and the towns along the river in those years
hardQuiz.e: Setting works as symbol in Hawthorne's allegory.

hardQuiz.q: Which set correctly matches title to author to genre or form?
o: “The Eve of St. Agnes” - Irving - short story
“The Fall of the House of Usher” - Keats - essay
hardQuiz.e: Twain's yarn is a tall tale; Keats's is a narrative poem; Poe's Usher is Gothic; Hawthorne's story is allegory.

hardQuiz.q: A student chooses to annotate “A tart temper never mellows with age” in Irving's description of Dame. Which annotation is the strongest?
o: It compares her scolding to something that never softens, reinforcing the sympathetic reading of Rip
It rhymes, which makes the line easy to memorize and repeat to a friend when preparing for the test on Tuesday
It is a complete sentence, which makes it a good quotation to put in a paper and a good sample of Irving's prose
It contains a verb, so it shows action in the story, which moves the plot forward and gives the reader something to watch
hardQuiz.e: Strong annotation names the device or effect and the purpose.

hardQuiz.q: All of the following are ways Poe builds mood in Usher's opening paragraph EXCEPT
o: Dark, heavy diction such as "dreary" and "melancholy"
The narrator's dread on first sight of the house
hardQuiz.e: The opening is descriptive narration, not dialogue.

hardQuiz.q: All of the following are ways Twain characterizes Jim Baker EXCEPT
o: By having the narrator state, "Baker was a coward"
Through the folksy dialect of his own speech
Through his confident claims about what jays can do
Through his stories about acorns and cabin roofs
hardQuiz.e: Baker is characterized through his speech and stories.

hardQuiz.q: Which best states the relationship between “The Eve of St. Agnes” and Usher according to the class's Haunted Palace lesson?
o: Both use inset texts, romance and mood to explore love, decay and the power of imagination
They share the same characters and settings, but in different years of the story
Both are comedies set in a small village and told in a playful, light style
Neither is a Romantic work, since both reject emotion, nature and imagination
hardQuiz.e: The class schedule asks how the texts relate; theme and mood links are key.

hardQuiz.q: Which sequence best shows Brown's changing attitude in “Young Goodman Brown”?
o: Confident resolve to go on his errand; growing doubt; shattering of faith; lifelong distrust
Lifelong distrust; confident resolve to go on his errand; growing doubt; a lasting peace
A lasting peace; lifelong distrust; confident resolve to go on his errand; growing doubt
Growing doubt; a lasting peace; confident resolve to go on his errand; lifelong distrust
hardQuiz.e: Brown is a dynamic character.

hardQuiz.q: Which best explains why Twain's frame (“Animals talk to each other, of course”) is significant?
o: It sets up the tall-tale premise and lets Twain distance himself while amusing the reader
It provides scientific proof that animals can speak to one another in language
It replaces the story of the jay with a lecture about the study of biology
It corrects Baker's grammar before the story about the jay begins
hardQuiz.e: The frame creates humor and irony.

hardQuiz.q: A student says the whole crowd of jays who each add a “leather-headed opinion” satirizes human behavior. This claim is best supported by which observation?
o: Twain compares the jays' arguing to “an average crowd of humans”
The jays fly south for the winter every year, as many birds do
The jays eat acorns and store them in trees for the winter months
The jays number five thousand at the cabin on that summer day
hardQuiz.e: Twain directly likens the jays to people.

hardQuiz.q: Which claim best combines Irving's characterization of Dame and Rip with his purpose? (pp. 34-38, 50)
o: By making Dame a termagant and Rip a beloved idler, Irving invites readers to laugh at domestic tyranny and to enjoy Rip's escape from it
Irving argues that all wives are tyrants and that a sensible man should avoid marriage altogether if he wants to be free of care
Irving proves that idleness makes Rip a hero of the Revolution and a model for others, who should follow him up into the hills
Irving shows that Dame Van Winkle is really a British spy who has been sent to watch Rip and to report on the village's plans
hardQuiz.e: Irving's ironic tone ("petticoat government") supports a humorous purpose.

hardQuiz.q: Which explains why the villagers call Rip a Tory? (p. 46)
o: His loyalty to the King marks him as out of step with the new republic he slept through
He works as an agent for the British army in the village and reports on the town
He hides a British flag in his house and refuses to remove it when asked
He demanded higher taxes at the inn on election day and made a scene
hardQuiz.e: The inn sign, flag and Federal/Democrat questions show the change.

hardQuiz.q: Which best explains the effect of the sign changing from George III to General Washington? (p. 45)
o: It symbolizes the shift from monarchy to republic in a single image while keeping the same face and setting
It shows that Rip needs glasses to read the new sign over the door of the inn, which has been repainted in blue and buff
It proves that the inn's owner was a soldier who fought in the war and has painted the sign himself in honor of his old general
It suggests that Rip has changed his own name while he was away on the mountain and no longer answers to the name Van Winkle
hardQuiz.e: The same portrait is "singularly metamorphosed" (p. 45).

hardQuiz.q: Which best explains why Hawthorne uses the phrase “Had Goodman Brown fallen asleep in the forest and only dreamed a wild dream? Be it so if you will”? (p. 68)
o: It leaves the events ambiguous so the reader focuses on the effects of doubt
It states that the forest events were certainly a dream, so nothing in them matters
It states that the forest events were certainly real, so the town is truly wicked
It reveals that the author himself was asleep while he was writing the story
hardQuiz.e: The ambiguity emphasizes Brown's changed life.

hardQuiz.q: The traveler says “I have a very general acquaintance here in New England.” This most strongly develops which idea? (p. 56)
o: The devil's reach extends to respected community leaders, suggesting hypocrisy at every level
The traveler is the governor of the colony in disguise, making his rounds of the towns to judge the mood of the people
The traveler is a merchant who trades with the towns of New England and knows a great many of the leading families there
The traveler is only seeking directions to Boston and is a bit lost in the woods, so he asks Brown to help him find the way
hardQuiz.e: He lists deacons, selectmen and members of the Great and General Court.

hardQuiz.q: Which of the following is the strongest evidence that Twain wants readers to see the jays as human? (pp. 137-138)
o: Baker says a jay can cry, laugh, feel shame, reason and plan, gossip and has a sense of humor
The jays build their nests in the tall trees of the forest above the cabin where Baker lives on his own
The jays eat acorns that they gather from the oaks around the clearing where the old empty cabin stands
The cabin has no ceiling between the rafters and the floor of the room, and one big room is all there is
hardQuiz.e: The direct list of human traits supports anthropomorphism.

hardQuiz.q: Which explains the comic effect of the jays' opinions about the hole? (p. 140)
o: Twain likens their arguments to an average crowd of humans, mocking human pomposity
The jays are completely silent as they look one by one into the hole in the roof
The jays disagree politely and take turns speaking in a calm and formal way
The jays copy Baker's speech and repeat his words back to him at the cabin
hardQuiz.e: The narrator compares the jays' "leather-headed opinions" to human opinions.

hardQuiz.q: Which best explains why Poe describes the house's reflection in the tarn as "remodeled and inverted" images? (p. 70)
o: The inverted reflection adds to the uncanny mood and foreshadows the house's fall into the tarn
It shows that the house is under construction by workers who are still building it
It proves that the tarn is dry in the summer and full of mud
It is a weather report about the way the clouds appear on the day
hardQuiz.e: The editors also call the inverted image in the tarn a deadly fateful image.

hardQuiz.q: Which best explains why the narrator of Usher reads the Mad Trist aloud? (p. 88)
o: He hopes the extremeness of the folly will relieve Roderick's excitement, but the story's noises seem to echo the house
He wants to cheer Madeline, who is recovering upstairs in her room, and hopes she will hear the tale through the wall
He wants to prove to Roderick that his fears are false and foolish by reading a story full of dragons and wild noise
He is practicing a performance that he plans to give at home in the spring, and has taken the old book down for the purpose
hardQuiz.e: He calls it a vague hope; the noises then match the story.

hardQuiz.q: According to the Introduction, which pairing of Poe and Hawthorne is most accurate?
o: Poe: single theatrical effect; Hawthorne: moral weight and the darkness of the soul
Poe: moral weight and depth of soul; Hawthorne: a single theatrical effect
Poe: humor and satire; Hawthorne: detective work and clues
Poe: local color and dialect; Hawthorne: impressionism and quick images
hardQuiz.e: The Introduction contrasts their darkness and their gifts.

hardQuiz.q: Which statement best links Twain's yarn to the Introduction's discussion of beast stories?
o: The yarn belongs to the old tradition of the beast fable revived in American local color and humor
The yarn is an example of Gothic horror in the style of Poe and his followers, with a ghostly setting and an ominous mood
The yarn is a detective story built on clues, reasoning and a final solution that reveals the truth about a crime in a cabin
The yarn is a Romantic ode that praises nature in elevated language and calls on the reader to admire the woods of the West
hardQuiz.e: The Introduction links it to Uncle Remus and Thurber's fables.

workedExamples.title: Identifying the Rhetorical Situation
workedExamples.prompt: A retired general publishes an op-ed in a national newspaper the week after a controversial military budget vote, urging Congress to reconsider. Identify SOAPSTone.
steps: Speaker: a retired general — someone with firsthand military authority, lending ethos
Occasion: the recent, controversial budget vote (this is the exigence)
Audience: Congress and newspaper-reading citizens who influence public opinion
Purpose: to persuade Congress to reconsider the budget decision
Subject: the military budget vote and its consequences
Tone: likely urgent and authoritative, given the speaker's background and timing
workedExamples.answer: Speaker=retired general (ethos); Occasion/exigence=the budget vote; Audience=Congress/public; Purpose=to persuade reconsideration; Subject=the budget vote; Tone=urgent, authoritative.

workedExamples.title: Naming and Explaining an Appeal
workedExamples.prompt: A nonprofit's ad says: 'Dr. Elena Ruiz, a pediatric surgeon with 20 years of experience, warns that delaying this legislation will cost children's lives.' Identify the appeals at work and their effect.
steps: Ethos: citing Dr. Ruiz's credentials (pediatric surgeon, 20 years) establishes her authority on the subject
Pathos: 'cost children's lives' evokes fear and urgency about vulnerable children
Logos is comparatively weak here — no data or statistics are cited
Effect: combining a credible expert's warning with emotionally charged stakes makes the claim feel both authoritative and urgent
workedExamples.answer: Primarily ethos (credentials) blended with pathos ('cost children's lives'), creating an authoritative and emotionally urgent warning.

workedExamples.title: Analyzing a Repetition Device
workedExamples.prompt: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills.' Identify the device and its effect.
steps: The phrase 'we shall fight' repeats at the start of each clause — this is anaphora
The repetition builds escalating intensity and resolve as each new location is added
The listing of locations (beaches, grounds, fields, streets, hills) suggests total, unwavering commitment
Effect: the device creates a rhythmic, almost unstoppable sense of determination, rallying the audience
workedExamples.answer: Anaphora ('we shall fight...'), which builds escalating resolve and rallies the audience through relentless repetition.

workedExamples.title: Analyzing Diction and Syntax Together
workedExamples.prompt: Compare: (A) 'The company terminated 200 employees.' (B) 'Two hundred families lost their livelihoods overnight.' Explain the rhetorical effect of the difference.
steps: Sentence A uses formal, corporate diction ('terminated,' 'employees') that feels clinical and distanced
Sentence B uses emotionally charged, concrete diction ('families,' 'livelihoods,' 'overnight') that personalizes the impact
Syntax: both are short declarative sentences, but B's word choices shift the emotional register dramatically
Effect: identical facts can be framed to minimize (A) or amplify (B) emotional impact purely through diction
workedExamples.answer: Diction alone shifts the tone from clinical/distanced (A) to emotionally personal and urgent (B), despite reporting the same event.

workedExamples.title: Turning Evidence into Commentary
workedExamples.prompt: Evidence: 'A 2023 study found that students who read 20 minutes daily scored 15% higher on reading assessments.' Write one sentence of commentary (not summary) using this evidence to support the claim that schools should mandate daily reading time.
steps: Summary would just restate the finding — that's not enough on its own
Commentary must explain WHY this evidence supports the specific claim about mandating reading time
Connect the statistic to the argument's stakes: what does a 15% gain mean for struggling readers specifically?
Example commentary: 'This 15% gain shows that even a small, consistent daily habit can meaningfully close achievement gaps — exactly the kind of low-cost intervention schools should be mandating.'
workedExamples.answer: Commentary example: 'This 15% gain shows even a small daily habit can meaningfully close achievement gaps — exactly why schools should mandate it.'

workedExamples.title: Writing a Concession and Rebuttal
workedExamples.prompt: Claim: schools should eliminate final exams. Write a one-sentence concession followed by a one-sentence rebuttal.
steps: Concession: acknowledge a fair point on the opposing side, e.g., that final exams can measure retention of a full semester's material
Rebuttal: explain why the writer's position still holds despite this valid point
Concession example: 'Final exams can, admittedly, reveal whether students retained material over a full semester.'
Rebuttal example: 'But a single high-stakes test rewards short-term cramming over the deep, lasting learning it claims to measure.'
workedExamples.answer: Concession: exams can measure semester-long retention. Rebuttal: but they reward cramming over the deep learning they claim to test.

workedExamples.title: Synthesizing Two Sources into One Point
workedExamples.prompt: Source A: 'Remote work increased reported employee satisfaction by 22%.' Source B: 'Companies with remote policies saw a 30% drop in office lease costs.' Write one synthesis sentence using both sources to support the claim that companies should adopt permanent remote work.
steps: Identify what each source contributes: A = employee benefit, B = financial benefit
A strong synthesis sentence combines them into ONE argument, not two separate summaries

Draft: 'Beyond the well-documented 22% rise in employee satisfaction (Source A), companies adopting remote work have also cut office lease costs by 30% (Source B) — evidence that the shift benefits both employees and the bottom line.'
This models proper citation-with-commentary, using two sources to build one unified point
workedExamples.answer: Example: 'Beyond the 22% rise in employee satisfaction (Source A), remote companies cut lease costs by 30% (Source B) — benefiting both employees and the bottom line.'

workedExamples.title: Writing a Device-to-Effect Sentence
workedExamples.prompt: A passage uses short, fragmented sentences ('No warning. No time. Just silence.') to describe a disaster's onset. Write a full rhetorical analysis sentence connecting this syntax to its effect.
steps: Identify the device: fragmented, staccato syntax
Identify the specific effect: mirrors the abruptness and disorientation of the disaster itself
Connect it to purpose: this makes the reader feel the shock the writer wants to convey, rather than just describing it
Draft: 'The fragmented syntax — “No warning. No time. Just silence.” — mimics the abruptness of the disaster itself, plunging the reader into the same disorientation the writer wants them to feel.'
workedExamples.answer: Example: 'The fragmented syntax mimics the disaster's abruptness, plunging the reader into the same disorientation the writer wants them to feel.'

workedExamples.title: Building a Nuanced Thesis
workedExamples.prompt: Prompt: 'Is competition beneficial to society?' Write a qualified, sophisticated thesis (not a simple yes/no).
steps: An absolute thesis ('competition is always good') is less sophisticated than a qualified one
Identify a meaningful condition under which the claim holds or doesn't

Draft: 'While competition drives innovation in economic markets, it becomes destructive when applied to systems — like healthcare or education — where cooperation, not rivalry, best serves the public good.'
This thesis is specific, arguable, and shows nuance by distinguishing between contexts
workedExamples.answer: Example: 'Competition drives innovation in markets, but becomes destructive in systems like healthcare or education, where cooperation better serves the public good.'

workedExamples.title: Fixing a Comma Splice and Checking Parallelism
workedExamples.prompt: Revise: 'The committee reviewed the proposal, they approved it unanimously, and are moving to sign, seal, and finalizing the contract.'
steps: First, identify the comma splice: 'reviewed the proposal, they approved it' joins two independent clauses with only a comma
Fix with a period or semicolon: 'The committee reviewed the proposal; they approved it unanimously.'
Next, check the list 'sign, seal, and finalizing' — 'finalizing' breaks parallel structure with 'sign' and 'seal'
Corrected: 'The committee reviewed the proposal; they approved it unanimously and are moving to sign, seal, and finalize the contract.'
workedExamples.answer: 'The committee reviewed the proposal; they approved it unanimously and are moving to sign, seal, and finalize the contract.'

workedExamples.title: Map the rhetorical situation with SOAPSTone
workedExamples.prompt: A retired general publishes an op-ed the week Congress debates the defense budget, urging lawmakers to fund veterans' health care before new weapons systems. Break down the rhetorical situation.
steps: Speaker: a retired general - high ethos on military matters, and a credible critic of defense spending priorities.
Occasion: the budget debate this week (kairos - a moment when the argument can actually influence a decision).
Audience: members of Congress and the voters who watch them, especially those who claim to support the troops.
Purpose: to persuade lawmakers to prioritize veterans' health funding over new weapons.
Subject: defense budget priorities. Tone: likely firm, disappointed, and morally serious.
workedExamples.answer: The general leverages insider ethos and precise timing (kairos) to press a 'support the troops' audience toward a specific budget choice.

workedExamples.title: Analyze an appeal, not just label it
workedExamples.prompt: A passage reads: 'I have buried men I trained. I have written the letters home. When I tell you this policy costs lives, I am not speculating.' Identify and analyze the appeal.
steps: The appeal is primarily ethos, reinforced by pathos.
The short, first-person clauses establish direct personal experience, positioning the speaker as a witness rather than a pundit.
'Buried men I trained' and 'written the letters home' carry heavy emotional weight, but their function is to authorize the claim that follows.
The final sentence converts that authority into a logical claim ('not speculating'), so the reader accepts the causal assertion.
Effect: the audience is inclined to trust the speaker's judgment and treat disagreement as callous.
workedExamples.answer: The writer builds credibility through lived experience and channels emotion into it, making the subsequent causal claim hard to dismiss.

workedExamples.title: Explain the effect of syntax and repetition
workedExamples.prompt: A passage: 'They took the land. They took the language. They took the names of the children and gave them new ones.' Analyze the rhetorical effect.
steps: The repeated subject-verb opening ('They took') is anaphora.
The parallel structure and mounting specificity (land, language, names of children) create a cumulative, escalating rhythm.
Asyndeton-like brevity - short, unconnected sentences - makes each loss land as a separate blow.
The final clause extends the pattern with an added consequence ('and gave them new ones'), breaking the rhythm to emphasize the deepest violation.
Effect: the passage builds a sense of relentless, systematic dispossession and moral outrage.
workedExamples.answer: Anaphora and parallel short sentences accumulate force; the broken final clause spotlights the gravest loss.

workedExamples.title: Name a precise tone and track a shift
workedExamples.prompt: A passage begins with wry, detached observations about a city council meeting ('another Tuesday, another three-hour debate about parking'), then shifts to: 'But behind the tedium, a family was about to lose its home.' Analyze the tone.
steps: Opening tone: wry and detached - the diction ('another Tuesday,' 'tedium') and the mundane subject signal amused impatience.
The pivot word 'But' marks a deliberate tonal shift.
The second sentence drops the irony for plain, weighty diction ('lose its home').
The shift reframes the 'tedium' as a moral failure of attention, not just boredom.
Effect: the reader is moved from detached amusement to discomfort, and the writer's real concern is revealed.
workedExamples.answer: The tone shifts from wry detachment to sober concern at 'But,' turning a joke about bureaucracy into an argument about consequences.

workedExamples.title: Turn summary into commentary
workedExamples.prompt: A student writes: 'The author notes that 60 percent of the town's water pipes are over a century old.' Add commentary that connects this evidence to a claim that the town has under-invested in basic infrastructure.
steps: Restate the evidence briefly (already done): 60 percent of pipes are 100+ years old.
Ask: what does this figure prove about the claim?
Connect: pipes that old are well past their design life, so a majority-aged system reflects decades of deferred maintenance.
Extend: this supports the claim that spending was diverted elsewhere while a core service decayed.
Result sentence: 'That most of the system predates living memory is not a quirk of history but evidence of sustained neglect: for generations, the town chose not to replace what it could not see.'
workedExamples.answer: Commentary explains that an aging majority of pipes demonstrates long-term deferred investment, directly supporting the under-investment claim.

workedExamples.title: Build a qualified thesis and outline the reasoning
workedExamples.prompt: Prompt: Should high schools start later in the morning? Draft a defensible, qualified thesis and a three-part line of reasoning.
steps: Take a position, but qualify it: later start times help most, but not without trade-offs.

Thesis: 'High schools should push start times to at least 8:30 a.m., because the sleep benefits for adolescents are well documented, provided districts adjust bus schedules and after-school activities to avoid shifting the burden onto working families.'
Sub-claim 1: adolescent biology - later melatonin release makes early starts counterproductive for learning.
Sub-claim 2: measurable outcomes - districts that shifted later report better attendance and fewer car crashes.
Sub-claim 3: the concession - transportation and childcare costs are real, so the policy must include a plan to manage them; this makes the argument more persuasive, not less.
workedExamples.answer: A qualified thesis plus a three-part line of reasoning (biology, outcomes, and a managed concession) gives the essay a clear spine.

workedExamples.title: Organize a synthesis paragraph by your claim
workedExamples.prompt: Synthesis prompt on whether cities should offer free public transit. You have Source A (ridership data), Source C (a budget analysis), and Source E (an equity argument). Draft one body paragraph organized around your claim.
steps: State your sub-claim first: free transit is justified primarily as an equity measure, and the fiscal cost is manageable.
Bring in Source E to establish the equity stakes: low-income residents spend a disproportionate share of income on fares.
Bring in Source A for support: pilot cities saw the largest ridership gains among riders who had previously walked long distances or skipped trips.
Bring in Source C to answer the obvious objection: the revenue loss is a small fraction of the transit budget and is partly offset by lower fare-collection costs.
Close the paragraph by tying the three back to your claim: the sources together show a targeted benefit at a bearable price.
workedExamples.answer: The paragraph leads with the writer's claim and recruits three sources to support and defend it, rather than summarizing each in turn.

workedExamples.title: Write a strong rhetorical analysis thesis
workedExamples.prompt: You are analyzing a commencement speech in which the speaker repeatedly contrasts 'the job you take' with 'the person you become,' uses self-deprecating anecdotes, and ends with a direct charge to the graduates. Draft a thesis.
steps: Do not list devices. Ask: what is the speaker doing overall, and to what end?
The speaker is redefining success for an audience anxious about careers, and lowering the stakes of failure.
Name the key moves that serve that purpose: the repeated antithesis, the humbling anecdotes, the closing charge.
Combine into an arguable claim about strategy and effect.

Thesis: 'By repeatedly setting external achievement against internal growth and undercutting his own resume with stories of failure, the speaker reframes success as character rather than career, freeing an anxious graduating class to take risks - a redefinition his final direct charge asks them to act on.'
workedExamples.answer: The thesis states what the speaker does (reframes success, lowers the cost of failure) and to what effect, previewing the analysis.

workedExamples.title: Use concede-then-counter in an argument
workedExamples.prompt: You are arguing that public libraries should expand evening hours. A reader objects that staffing costs are already strained. Write a concede-then-counter passage.
steps: Acknowledge the objection fairly and specifically: 'The concern about staffing is legitimate; many library systems have cut positions over the past decade and cannot simply add shifts.'
Grant that it constrains the solution: 'Any expansion must be designed around that reality rather than ignoring it.'

Counter by limiting the objection's force: 'But evening demand is concentrated in a few branches and a few hours, so a targeted extension - two branches, three nights a week - would cost far less than a system-wide change.'
Add support: 'Pilot programs elsewhere covered the cost by shifting, not adding, hours, opening later and closing later on those nights.'
Return to the thesis: 'A narrow, evidence-based expansion answers the staffing worry instead of being defeated by it.'
workedExamples.answer: The passage concedes the staffing point, then narrows the proposal so the objection no longer defeats it, strengthening the writer's credibility.

workedExamples.title: Revise a wordy sentence for the MC 'writing' skill
workedExamples.prompt: Revise: 'Due to the fact that the committee was not able to reach a consensus decision, it was decided that the vote would be postponed until a later date.'
steps: 'Due to the fact that' is padding for 'because.'
'consensus decision' is redundant; 'consensus' or 'agreement' suffices.
'it was decided that' is passive and vague; name the actor or drop it.
'postponed until a later date' is redundant; 'postponed' already means to a later time.
Assemble the concise version.
workedExamples.answer: 'Because the committee could not agree, it postponed the vote.'

workedExamples.title: Analyzing Twain's anthropomorphism in "Baker's Bluejay Yarn"
workedExamples.prompt: In a well-developed paragraph, explain how Twain uses anthropomorphism and Jim Baker's point of view to advance a theme in "Baker's Bluejay Yarn".
steps: Claim: Twain gives the bluejays human speech and behavior, and lets Jim Baker narrate in a folksy voice, to suggest that human effort and pride can be as absurd as the jay's.
Evidence: choose the knothole tale (the jay dropping acorns into the hole) and one line of Baker's confident, dialect-heavy commentary; cite with author, title and page.
Commentary 1: explain that anthropomorphism makes the jays' failure feel like a human one, so the joke doubles as a metaphor for futile effort.
Commentary 2: explain how Baker's serious, sincere tone (indirect characterization) juxtaposed with the ridiculous story creates humor and irony and builds his credibility.
Link: tie back to purpose. Twain uses humor to reflect on the foolishness in human society of his time (1835-1880).
workedExamples.answer: Twain uses anthropomorphism and Baker's sincere voice to turn a comic animal story into a commentary on human folly. When the jay keeps dropping acorns into the knothole, its stubborn effort mirrors human persistence in the face of futility, and the juxtaposition of Baker's earnest tone with an absurd tale invites the reader to laugh at both. The humor therefore serves Twain's purpose: to gently mock human pride.

workedExamples.title: Allusion and setting in "Young Goodman Brown"
workedExamples.prompt: In what ways is Hawthorne's use of setting and allusion in "Young Goodman Brown" significant? Answer in one cohesive response with evidence.
steps: Claim: Hawthorne moves Brown from Puritan Salem into a dark forest and layers in Biblical allusions to show that evil hides inside the very community that claims to be godly.
Setting evidence: contrast the ordered village and Faith's pink ribbons with the shadowy forest path; label the mood and the words that create it.
Allusion evidence: the traveler's serpent-like staff (Eden) and the forest communion; explain what each reference suggests about temptation and hypocrisy.
Commentary: explain how setting and allusion together push Brown's shift from trusting to distrustful and support the theme of lost faith.
Link: end on Hawthorne's critical view of Puritan hypocrisy and the story's ambiguity.
workedExamples.answer: Hawthorne uses the shift from the ordered village to the dark forest, along with allusions such as the serpent-like staff, to argue that evil is hidden inside Puritan society itself. The setting shows Brown moving away from the safety of community, while the Biblical references frame his choice as a moral fall. By the end, Brown's lasting distrust proves how much damage suspicion of others can do.

workedExamples.title: Which device? Answering a “which is present” question
workedExamples.prompt: Which literary device is present in: “A tart temper never mellows with age, and a sharp tongue is the only edged tool that grows keener with constant use”?
steps: Identify the comparison: a tongue is compared to an edged tool without using like or as.
Rule out simile (no like/as), personification (the tongue is not given human traits), and hyperbole (not an obvious exaggeration).
Name the device: metaphor. Explain the effect: it warns of Dame's constant scolding and helps the reader sympathize with Rip.
workedExamples.answer: Metaphor. Irving compares a scolding tongue to a tool that only gets sharper with use, characterizing Dame Van Winkle as harsh and unchanging.

workedExamples.title: Word in context: vocabulary from Rip Van Winkle
workedExamples.prompt: In “Rip Van Winkle”, Irving describes Dame Van Winkle as a “termagant.” What does the word most nearly mean, and how do you know?
steps: Read the sentence and note the context: Dame scolds Rip and is described as having a tart temper.
Guess a meaning from context (a scolding, bad-tempered woman), then check against the definition: violent, overbearing, quarrelsome woman.
Choose the answer that matches in both meaning and tone (negative), not a mild word like 'merchant' or 'neighbor'.
workedExamples.answer: A violent, overbearing, quarrelsome woman. The scolding context and negative tone show it is an insult.

workedExamples.title: Chronology: ordering events in Usher
workedExamples.prompt: Put these Usher events in order: the house collapses; the narrator arrives; the narrator reads the Mad Trist; Madeline is entombed; Madeline appears at the door.
steps: Start with the narrator's arrival in response to Roderick's letter.
Madeline appears to die and is entombed in the vault.
Days later the narrator reads the Mad Trist; sounds match the story; Madeline appears; the house collapses.
